talks.title: 2016 - Sean Jackson (74rku5) - Oooh! We've Had An Incident! How Should We Respond
talks.teaser: Maps a six-phase response lifecycle from preparation to closure, with regulatory duties and tamper-evident chain-of-custody.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames incident response planning as operational debt organizations owe when they hold customer, financial, or health data. It walks through a six-phase lifecycle—preparation, identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and closure—rather than ad hoc firefighting after something breaks.

Preparation covers synchronized time across sites, login banners aligned with HR and legal, centralized protected logging (including duplicate local and aggregate copies), one-person-one-account conventions, emergency privileged accounts with alerting, jump bags for remote sites, out-of-band team communications, help-desk triage training, rotating cross-functional response teams, tabletop drills, and advance policy choices such as watch-and-learn versus pulling the plug. Identification stresses calm intake, full documentation from the first report, paired handlers, baseline comparison, and a formal decision to declare an incident. Containment addresses staged notifications with need-to-know discipline, factual communications, network-level isolation without destroying evidence, and broad artifact collection.

Later phases cover root-cause analysis (including repeated “why” questioning), wiping systems when rootkits are suspected, enterprise-wide hardening and prioritized vulnerability scans before closure, operational validation and tightened monitoring, and management sign-off with lessons learned fed back into preparation. The speaker also estimates breach cost from staff hours and dwell time, classifies impact types, surveys GLBA, HIPAA, HITECH, SOX, PCI DSS, and state breach duties, and describes digital chain of custody using hashes, working copies, and tamper-evident storage.

talks.teaser: War stories from the help desk highlight everyday IT failures and the operational lessons they leave behind.
talks.summary:
The presentation is framed as comic relief for a security audience by a generalist systems administrator who collects operational disasters from personal experience and colleagues. It opens with familiar tropes—company-wide email storms, delayed HR account provisioning, and backup restores derailed when a novice corrupts the only copies—before longer anecdotes tied to specific situations.

Several detailed cases stand alone. A college music teacher’s overheating Mac turns out to be foam stuffed into fans, melting the CPU after help desk tickets were ignored. A Hong Kong rollout hits a ten-user connection ceiling because the Windows NT server was the MSDN-limited build, forcing a multi-day rebuild. At Honeywell Aerospace, a remote operator issues a destructive crontab command; only a recent cron backup restores scheduled jobs. A retail upgrade coincides with a dead router and an emergency parts run. At Charles Schwab, an Infoblox DNS/DHCP migration allegedly inserts a duplicate record that makes schwab.com unreachable until vendor root access repairs the database.

The speaker closes with non-technical commentary on Wells Fargo leadership and sales-goal policy, then encourages conference attendance and cybersecurity awareness resources. Practitioners should hear repeated lessons: verify licensing and vendors, lock workstations, heed user complaints, and keep backups—including configuration like cron—before trusting shared access or new appliances.

talks.title: 2016 - Josh Dustin (@joshdustin) - They used my own method to own my account
talks.teaser: A CSO recounts Amazon account takeover via reused Adobe passwords and clearing his teen son of planted online evidence.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with the 2013 Adobe breach dump: roughly 150 million records, encrypted password blobs that have resisted full key recovery, and cleartext hints. By sorting duplicate ciphertext and aligning hints—such as 1.9 million accounts sharing one hash where the top hint is “one to six”—attackers can infer many passwords without cracking encryption, including a worked example around hints like “metal” and periodic-table references.

The narrative turns personal when a suspicious Amazon order arrives at his home. His wife’s password for their shared account matches one exposed in the Adobe data years earlier, illustrating how breach-derived guessing can own live accounts. Weeks later, a 2 a.m. call accuses his fourteen-year-old of running a doxing and swatting persona online. Twitter drama, reverse image search, recycled jokes, old IP logs, and a SET screenshot make the case look damning until lake-trip timestamps show the accused account still posting while the son had no phone access.

Practitioners should treat hint collisions as a practical risk in old breaches, enforce unique passwords across household services, and remember that open social posts can be weaponized as planted linkage. The closing notes how others verified the real operator using a browser WebRTC issue before law enforcement involvement.

talks.title: 2016 - Andrew Brandt (Spike) - Ingress Egress: The emerging threats of AR gaming
talks.teaser: Shows how an AR game's network traffic, player-tracking databases and GPS spoofing expose players to stalking and cheating.
talks.summary:
Andrew Brandt, a threat researcher, examines Ingress, the augmented reality game whose player-submitted location data later supported Pokémon Go. Using a lab setup that decrypts SSL traffic from a phone, he shows what the app sends to and receives from publisher servers. He covers Google-based login, a startup check-in that returns inventory and game rules, and calls to analytics and payment services that receive device details such as model, carrier and IMEI. He also describes location data sent over a cell-tower-based protocol, and a constant stream of other players' activity that the client receives even when it is not displayed.

The middle of the talk covers how that stream is abused. Third-party databases index the traffic and let players track others' habits, portal holdings and play areas, which has been used to harass people. Brandt describes GPS spoofing on Android with the Xposed framework, bots that farm gear and sell it, and an emulator tool that teleports the game to any point on a map. He recounts losing a guardian portal he had held for 262 days to a spoofed player shortly after mentioning its age to a faction member.

He closes by comparing Pokémon Go, which does not broadcast chat, and proposes fixes: dropping player names from action messages, banning people rather than accounts, tracing item trades between accounts, and handling stalking reports better. He asks the audience for further ideas to pass to the publisher, which he says has not responded to his outreach.

talks.title: 2016 - Chris Larsen - Phishing with Dynamite
talks.teaser: Shows how ambiguous new top-level domains and browser address bars can turn a plain-text email into a convincing phish.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the crowded domain market that followed the expansion of top-level domains. With good names already taken, registries opened hundreds of new extensions, many sold at low prices. The speaker's team found several of these extensions where nearly every site in their web logs was spam, scam or malware, and noted that blocking them outright may catch a few innocent sites.

The central problem is ambiguity. A string like zip can mean a file archive or a domain, and browser address bars have to guess which one a user meant. Words such as dat can also be read as domains, so Java class names can collide with new extensions. The team found roughly one collision for every 150 classes in Apache Tomcat and HTTP components code. They then built a phishing scenario: a plain-text email cited a real Java vulnerability and asked developers to look it up. Pasting that text into the address bar sent them to a fake search page, and 17 of 18 senior Java developers at a cooperating software company who reached it clicked through.

The advice is to tell staff not to click links on suspicious extensions, whether they arrive by email, text message or search result. Hovering over an internationalized domain shows its encoded form, which can expose lookalikes. Developers should know that class names can collide with domain names in any language, and that some extensions may be worth blocking entirely.

talks.title: 2016 - Chad Butler - Big Shop AppSec for Everyone Else
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning 2016 - Chad Butler - Big Shop AppSec for Everyone Else.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Chad Butler, Managing Director of Security Services at Caliber Security Partners, addresses the challenges smaller software shops and startups face when attempting to establish an application security (AppSec) program. Startups frequently build great software products only to see critical deals stalled by enterprise prospective customers' security teams demanding compliance with exhaustive questionnaires and stringent requirements. Drawing on historical data from the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report showing web applications as the persistent leading source of breaches, Butler explains that traditional AppSec approaches designed for waterfall development fail to keep up with modern agile and rapid deployment cadences. He outlines practical, cost-effective strategies for smaller organizations to build an effective AppSec posture, satisfy enterprise vendor audits, and integrate security directly into developer workflows.

### Key Topics
- **Vendor Security Assessments and Overcoming the "Special Snowflake" Problem**: Large enterprises often hit suppliers with 30-page security questionnaires that pile on irrelevant or unused security controls. Butler advises teams to "plant the flag and declare success" by proactively choosing and justifying recognized frameworks before enterprise customers impose arbitrary requirements. He highlights Boeing's publicly available vendor security questionnaire on SafeCode's website (Principles for Software Assurance Assessment) and alignment with standards like ISO 27034 as strong baselines.
- **Rethinking Threat Modeling**: Traditional multi-hour whiteboard threat modeling sessions developed under waterfall frameworks often cause developer friction and fail in fast-paced sprint cycles or multi-daily release environments. Butler advocates replacing or augmenting them with pragmatic, lightweight approaches.
- **Winning Developer Hearts and Minds**: AppSec programs fail when security teams adopt a "my way or the highway" approach. Security teams must reduce friction, meet developers where they work (e.g., inside Jira rather than forcing separate portals), provide actionable solutions rather than just problems, and offer engaging incentives.

### Technical Details
- **Task-Level Threat Assessments**: A lightweight mechanism implemented directly into backlog or defect trackers (such as Jira). Developers answer an eight-question checklist covering areas like sensitive data, authentication, authorization, password resets, cryptography, and third-party libraries. If any response is "yes," the workflow assigns specific application security controls as acceptance criteria for that task, embedding security validation into developer and QA testing while providing an auditable metric of reviewed features.
- **Standardized Security Requirements**: Grounding development and QA requirements in established standards such as OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard) and the CWE/SANS Top 25 Monster Mitigations list. Storing requirements and stack-specific implementation guides in team wikis allows developers to adapt code patterns to their specific frameworks.
- **Interactive Training**: Avoiding expensive, passive training in favor of hands-on exploitation and remediation labs using deliberately vulnerable applications (e.g., WebGoat, BeEF). Motivation can be driven through gamified recognition systems, such as Adobe's martial arts belt system (white to black belt), custom challenge coins, or helmet stickers.
- **Tooling and Testing Strategy**: Focusing on pragmatic testing rather than expensive enterprise platforms (e.g., a $300 Burp Suite Pro license in skilled hands instead of a $40,000 scanner). Implementing tools like ThreadFix to aggregate vulnerability results from static/dynamic testing and automatically sync defect tracking with Jira.

### Takeaways
Organizations should adopt Paul Graham's startup philosophy to "do things that don't scale" when beginning AppSec: start small by tackling a single vulnerability class (like cross-site scripting or SQL injection), track progress in simple spreadsheets or dashboards, and gradually formalize the practice. Proactive adoption of standard baselines, lightweight task-level gating, and developer-first collaboration yield significantly better security outcomes than heavyweight, obstructive gates. Finally, while stopgaps like Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) provide temporary protection, they should never serve as a permanent replacement for secure coding.

The session opens by crediting volunteers and sponsors who scaled the event to roughly seven hundred attendees, many of them first-timers. Troy Jessup traces roughly fifteen years of SAINTCON history, including a shift about four and a half years ago from invite-only gatherings to an open registration model that outgrew badge and venue planning.

Practical guidance covers Twitter as the official channel, an online schedule, session recordings on YouTube after the conference, split lunch lines, and Wi-Fi badge assembly with a Thursday afternoon distribution for spare parts. He surveys major activities: the pre-con hackers challenge and its winners, the main challenge game with a lifetime black badge prize, lockpick village instruction, an upgraded Vault physical security room, hardware hacking village badge builds, and new HHB labs with guided exercises on tools such as HackRF and SDR gear.

Additional offerings include red versus blue network competition seating, badge modification and password cracking contests, and a Hack in the Box hacker space open late. The talk closes with provisional dates for the next conference and a likely return to the Utah Valley Convention Center, plus renewed thanks to sponsors who funded expansions like the Vault.

He says it matched what he expected: a smaller, industry-focused event with strong discussions and a knowledgeable, resilient community. His favourite part was the village areas, including the tamper evident, lockpicking and safe cracking villages, where attendees openly shared how to work through the tasks.

He explains that the nickname came from his company's CEO after an early lab project in which he rewrote part of a botnet to take over security cameras and turn them into cryptocurrency miners. He describes mostly working on the defensive side as a blue teamer. His route into security was unusual: he started as a musician, then spent about 20 years as a system administrator before a digital forensics class taught by the CEO pushed him into the industry.

He also describes his current work as an educator who builds modular, hands-on training for organisations, with realistic networks and scenarios, including ransomware detonations that blue teamers must then investigate. He closes by saying he hopes to try the badge RPG before the event ends, and that he enjoys talking about music, puzzles and game culture with anyone who approaches him.

Xanadu has attended for about six years, started out volunteering and is now on staff, working registration, where attendees must finish every sign-up step before they get a badge. A favourite moment is opening the doors on the first day and seeing new faces arrive.

Outside SAINTCON, Xanadu runs the auction and raffle for BSides Idaho Falls and organises that event. During the pandemic, a joint virtual BSides event covered both Boise and Idaho Falls. A nonprofit, the Eastern Idaho Cyber Education Alliance, helps fund these events. Xanadu also does woodworking, including a box with an X and 2600 on its front that has travelled between hacker conferences, a colour-coded table with epoxy sides and an acrylic top, and a commissioned piece for a university teacher that has a covered dog nook.

The conversation traces how Xanadu joined the community twelve years ago, when a CTF trip to DEF CON meant looking after a son too young to attend. That experience showed the scene is about people and networking. The family now attends conferences together, and Xanadu recalls the son making his own choice when offered alcohol at DEF CON and a daughter who uses social engineering skills in nursing. The chat closes with an invitation to approach Xanadu on any topic and thanks for the volunteer work.

talks.summary:
Ben, known by the handle Malus, sits down for a short hallway interview at SAINTCON. He explains that the name came from a joke with fellow red teamers, who asked what a bad guy would be called in Latin, drawing on the Latin he studied during his Catholic schooling. He has about 17 years in information security, though hacking has occupied only the last four or five of them.

His path began with networking after he enlisted in the Marine Corps at 18. He moved from tactical networking into defensive cyber work, which is blue team, and later switched to offensive work once the Marine Corps built out an offensive cyber unit. He credits his father, who has worked in networking and security for his whole career, as a major influence, and the two bonded over technical discussions. He says he pushed to be placed in the networking role when he enlisted.

This was his first SAINTCON. He had hoped to attend through his service, but funding delays meant he volunteered to run the lockpick village instead, which also gave him a way to give back to a community that had helped him. He said he had an intermediate grasp of lockpicking beforehand and learned a lot working with the village team, and he recalled teaching a visitor to escape a pair of handcuffs. He closed by saying he plans to return every year.

The conversation then moves to how Chandler got into security: by accident, after starting out in biological engineering with no computing background, when a classmate pushed a capture-the-flag event at Utah State University.

Chandler explains that early CTF challenges were learned by piecing problems together one at a time, and credits the student who pulled them into that first meeting. Today Chandler works in cyber threat intelligence and spends much of free time running a student security group at Utah State. About 25 members compete in CTFs and weekly meetings draw 30 to 60 people, with larger speaker events around twice a month.

The interview closes with outdoor hobbies such as motorcycles, skiing and rock climbing, and with the value of mentoring students early in their careers. The practical takeaway is the emphasis on connecting newcomers to the community and helping them find a place in a field that has room for different interests.

The conversation opens with how hallway interviews at SAINTCON began while the event was planning a virtual edition in 2020. Organizers heard that many attendees felt isolated despite large crowds, so short profiles were meant to surface shared interests and give people an easy reason to say hello in the hallways. The format continued in person after a rough early attempt with a small 360 camera.

The middle turns to what Pope does outside the day job: a heavily segmented home network with many VLANs, family Minecraft, honeypots, and telemetry pulled into several analytics platforms for work demonstrations. He describes chasing an endpoint alert caused by legitimate video-editing software launching PowerShell to open an external link, and how prior breach news pushed him toward stricter micro-segmentation and IoT egress allow lists.

The close is personal and reflective: time with kids, a thought experiment about rebuilding after societal collapse, beliefs about free will and refusing to treat people as NPCs, and cautious excitement about AI tooling and autonomous systems. Pope invites connection through dinosaurs and home-lab talk, and frames repeated failure as how he improves.

talks.summary:
The talk opens with how the speaker picked up the handle Spike, a nickname that replaced the one he had chosen on his first day at a Mac magazine. He then traces his start in hacking on TRS-80 and Commodore 64 machines in the early 1980s, when the craft meant cracking game copy protection and swapping in a crew name in the credits. Despite an English degree rather than a technical one, he taught himself and argues that strong writing paired with technical skill is rare and valuable.

He describes moving from reviewing hardware at PC World to covering computer crime. A late feature on browser toolbars used packet captures to trace how affiliate ads from major retailers ended up in those toolbars, and the reporting pushed the online ad industry toward proof that ad spend reached its intended destination. That work led him to malware research and network forensics, and then to a job after a conversation on the Black Hat show floor. He walks the three-pane interface, stresses legal and employer policy limits on sniffing, and shows how display filters shrink huge pcaps before analysis. Examples cover spotting abnormal SSH sessions via conversation statistics, establishing traffic baselines so Roku broadcasts are not mistaken for malware, and using TLS pre-master secret logs to decrypt HTTPS flows locally. talks.teaser: Follows Black Basta ransomware intrusions from phishing entry to the tools used, with detection ideas for defenders.
talks.summary:
This talk profiles the Black Basta ransomware group, which appeared around April 2022 and uses double extortion: it encrypts victims' files and threatens to leak stolen data. The speaker, a threat analyst at Mandiant, explains how activity was grouped into clusters, why attribution is difficult, and how one cluster was later found to be a merge of nine earlier clusters. Public reporting on the victim count is covered, along with the speaker's own figures of 39 intrusions across 21 industry verticals.

The middle of the talk focuses on the most active cluster and its initial access, which came almost entirely from a modular backdoor run as a botnet. Operators sometimes used infected machines to phish new victims, including by replying inside existing email threads with malicious files. The talk then walks through the tooling seen across intrusions: BloodHound and AdFind for Active Directory reconnaissance, a PowerShell port scanner, Cobalt Strike Beacon for command and control, SystemBC as a tunneler, and remote management software such as AnyDesk for persistence. For each, the speaker suggests detection ideas, including alerting on SMB scanning, placing honeypot objects in Active Directory, checking code signing, flagging rundll32 loading unusual file extensions, watching for odd top-level domains, and blocking remote management relay domains.

The closing part covers the group's return after a summer pause, when the botnet behind its access was disrupted by a law enforcement takedown. The operators shifted to other malware families and kept running phishing campaigns, and a new cluster was created for recent intrusions. The takeaways are that phishing remains effective, user education should include the fact that trusted email threads can carry malicious content, and pre-ransomware activity can be detected.

talks.title: Hallway
talks.teaser: A SAINTCON volunteer covers founding a Las Vegas DEF CON group, a puzzle-box contest, and entering infosec.
talks.summary:
AJ, who is volunteering at SAINTCON for a second year, explains how the event's welcoming community drew them back. About 13 years ago, after starting a QA job, they attended DEF CON 20 at a partner's suggestion and found that the field offered more to learn than they could ever exhaust. They later co-founded a Las Vegas DEF CON group with a partner after earlier local groups had faded. The weekly Wednesday meetup draws 15 to 30 people, mostly at a bar, with others at a hacker space and a local red team building.

Beyond the group, AJ staffs BSides Las Vegas and works as a photo goon at DEF CON. AJ also built a puzzle-box contest at DEF CON, a 30x30 cube with compartments that each led to the next, ending in a pay phone whose number players had to find and call. Clues were kept vague on purpose, hints went to teams that got stuck, and one team won. A harder version is planned for next year. Personal projects include a local AI setup that needs a lot of RAM, along with ideas for a mini badge, car hacking and healthcare topics.

The conversation closes with a practical point for newcomers: if AJ does not know an answer to a question, they will point the person to someone who does. The takeaway is that the local community is open to new people and that volunteering is a good way to meet them.

talks.title: 2023 - Bryce Kunz
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers move through cloud accounts by abusing phishing, CloudFormation deployment links and exposed storage buckets.
talks.summary:
The talk lays out a cloud red team approach for the major providers, moving from reconnaissance to initial access and post-exploitation, and switching between control plane and data plane access. Entry points include web application bugs that expose instance metadata credentials, globally shared machine images that may hold secrets, and client-side attacks that steal browser sessions. Adversary-in-the-middle phishing can hijack single sign-on sessions, but phishing-resistant hardware tokens with web authentication block it by checking the domain.

The main case abuses a CloudFormation quick-create link. A victim who deploys a template hosted in an attacker-controlled S3 bucket unknowingly creates a role with admin permissions that trusts the attacker's account. A custom resource backed by a Lambda function reports the victim's account ID to an API Gateway the attacker owns. Redirectors and CloudFront failed because the template URL must point to S3 or amazonaws.com. To find candidate buckets, the speaker wrote a serverless scanner that guessed names and found about 10 world-writable buckets over roughly five days.

The closing advice centers on defense and learning. Routing stack deployments through a strict CI/CD pipeline limits this abuse, and the speaker was not aware of a built-in control that requires extra approval before a deployment. He also pointed to vulnerable cloud labs and permission-mapping tools for practice.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this SAINTCON "Hallway" interview, a security professional named Kyle speaks about his entry into the cybersecurity field, his career progression, and his extensive involvement with community-driven conference villages and competitions. Kyle outlines how early hands-on troubleshooting led him to meet industry mentors, attend conferences like SAINTCON, and eventually manage major physical security and social engineering tracks.

### Key Topics
- **Career Path and Mentorship**: Kyle started out repairing laptops and handling general IT tasks. When tasked with networking a store's point-of-sale (POS) system without prior infrastructure, he learned by trial and error. An acquaintance encouraged him to apply for a security position, leading him to meet Kevin Howard (kho). Under Kevin's mentorship, Kyle transitioned from a security analyst role into security engineering, DevOps, and related positions.
- **The SAINTCON Vault**: Introduced to SAINTCON around 2018 by Kevin Howard, Kyle learned foundational physical security skills such as lock picking and soldering. He eventually took over organizing "The Vault," a physical security challenge village. The Vault annually features humorous themes honoring Kevin Howard—such as Cheap Sheep Enterprises, the Howard Family Vault (Indiana Jones-style Jade Idol retrieval), and the Howard Motel—along with intentionally unsolved "impossible mode" challenges.
- **Social Engineering Community (DEF CON)**: Kyle describes co-running DEF CON's Social Engineering Community (SEC), originally conceived by Snow, Offensive, JC, and Stephanie. He highlights the logistical challenges of building soundproof calling booths, transporting flight cases, managing disruptions like a hotel bomb scare, and hosting themed vishing competitions.

### Technical Details
- **Physical Security & Vault Challenges**: The Vault incorporates varied bypass and entry challenges, including lock picking, shimming, under-the-door tools, and canned air bypasses for Request to Exit (REX) sensors. To keep participants challenged, organizers feature an unsolved "white whale door" without known vulnerabilities. Past challenges included the Kaba X-09 high-security dial lock, while the current iteration introduces standalone ATMs to see if contestants can access the cash compartment.
- **Social Engineering Tactics**: In DEF CON's "A Slice of Deception" competition, participants targeted pizza companies (e.g., Papa Murphy's, Papa John's). Contestants deployed varied pretexting techniques, costume changes (such as delivery drivers or factory workers), and background audio effects (e.g., ambient keyboard typing sounds) from soundproof phone booths to extract information.
- **Hardware & Software Projects**: Outside of conference work, Kyle conducts Black Hat Python training, builds Python automation scripts, works with AWS, and attempts home automation projects, such as retrofitting window blinds with hardwired servo motors.

### Takeaways
Kyle emphasizes that community involvement and safe practice environments are critical for developing defensive and offensive skill sets. While outsiders might question teaching techniques like lock picking or phone-based deception, Kyle notes that understanding adversary methodologies directly enables defenders to build more resilient controls. He encourages conference attendees to experiment across diverse domains—including physical security, Python programming, cloud engineering, and social engineering.

talks.title: 2023 - Kenton McDaniel - Quantifying Cyber Risk in Real Dollars
talks.teaser: Shows how to express exposed services and excess admin rights as dollar risk so executives can prioritize remediation.
talks.summary:
Kenton McDaniel argues that critical, high, medium and low ratings fail to show business leaders which risks deserve attention. He proposes expressing remaining cyber risk in dollars tied to what an organization earns or spends, accepting that such figures will never be exact. Generic industry breach-cost averages rarely fit a particular company, so the analyst must first understand its finances.

Through a series of hypothetical companies, he works through several scenarios. An exposed remote desktop port on an isolated server holding non-critical data is judged low-impact once context is added, with an estimated loss of about $50,000 for restoring the machine. In another case, 60% of users hold domain administrator rights, which he says could erase the entire annual profit, so he suggests reducing the number of domain admins and using very long, vaulted passwords. A cloud-hosted WordPress site with SSH open to the internet, privileged containers and customer personal data is framed around reputational harm and recovery time. A final identity provider case, with unrestricted geolocation access and weak user awareness, is estimated at around $100,000.

The closing advice is that risk can never be driven to zero, so the acceptable level must be agreed with stakeholders. Expect dollar figures to be poorly received at first, and avoid fear, uncertainty and doubt, which loses credibility quickly. Always bring a remediation, even one costing more than the risk, and start with quick wins to build trust through data. Shutting a service down can be a valid fix.

talks.title: 2023 - Sam Moses - Easy Wins to Make My Job Harder
talks.teaser: Walks through common internal network attack paths, from LLMNR poisoning and SMB relay to ADCS abuse, with matching defenses.
talks.summary:
Sam Moses, a penetration tester, shares an attacker's view of internal network security, built around two attack paths he has used repeatedly on recent engagements. The first starts with a man-in-the-middle position on a network that still uses LLMNR or NBT-NS. Responder poisons those name requests to capture credentials, which are relayed over SMB to hosts without required signing. A relayed local admin account can then expose plaintext domain admin credentials through an LSA dump. Recommended fixes include disabling both legacy protocols once DNS is confirmed, requiring SMB signing, limiting local admin reuse, and applying least privilege.

The second path begins with null sessions, which let an attacker enumerate usernames and the password policy. Password spraying, kept under the lockout threshold, finds accounts with weak passwords. From a domain user, an AD CS web enrollment misconfiguration (ESC8) can be abused by relaying NTLM authentication to obtain a certificate, which leads to an administrator hash and domain-wide access. Mitigations include restricting anonymous enumeration, removing unneeded certificate services, disabling NTLM on domain controllers, alerting on spraying patterns, and using long passwords with a password manager and separate admin accounts.

Throughout, he stresses defense in depth: fixing one path still leaves others open. He notes that red and blue teams share the goal of making attacks too costly to continue.

talks.title: 2023 - James Cabe
talks.teaser: Presents an isolated recovery environment design for rebuilding networks after a cyber attack, with open-source tooling.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that organizations will eventually be compromised, so the real question is how quickly they can recover. The speaker, who has spent years on incident response and cleanup for industrial and oil and gas clients, argues that backups and disaster recovery sites often mirror the compromised environment, so they offer little protection. He says recovery planning has to identify the minimal set of crown jewel services, such as DNS, routing and authentication servers, that keep a site running.

The core proposal is an isolated recovery environment: a small, self-contained unit that can be disconnected from the network and brought up in a known-good state. He described a design built on a small embedded appliance with cellular connectivity, separate management and data-plane interfaces, and an encrypted disk whose keys sit in a TPM. Virtual machines and containers are rebuilt automatically at boot. Hosts are moved onto a clean network only after static, dynamic and network analysis finds them clean, and unusual traffic can send a host back to quarantine. He also covered running tools as containers, reverting a jump box to a known hash, and setting up a war room on clean laptops that do not rely on the affected environment.

He closed by saying he plans to publish the scripts and slides on GitHub. The work grew out of helping small towns and cities that lack any recovery capability, and he plans a hands-on resilience exercise at DEF CON. The takeaways are to assume compromise, cut off suspect systems early, keep recovery tooling immutable and separate, and rehearse recovery ahead of time.

talks.title: 2023 - Lee Christensen, Will Schroeder, and Maxwell Harley - Fighting Data With Data
talks.teaser: Presents Nemesis, an open-source platform that automatically enriches data collected during offensive engagements.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the repetitive work red teamers face after pulling files from a target. A downloaded .NET assembly has to be copied to a Windows analysis machine for decompilation, an encrypted Office document needs its hash extracted and cracked on a separate rig, and most offensive tool output is unstructured text. Data also stays siloed across several C2 frameworks and individual laptops, so teammates lack a shared view of an assessment.

The speakers introduce Nemesis, a Kubernetes-based data processing platform. Connectors send data from C2 frameworks to a web API, which queues it for enrichment services. Those services extract text from Office files, convert documents to PDF, scan for credentials, check .NET binaries for deserialization primitives, and decompile assemblies. Results are stored in Elasticsearch and PostgreSQL, surfaced in a dashboard, and sent to Slack when something notable turns up. Demos cover a Chrome extension that uploads documents, automatic cracking of an encrypted zip's hash against a small wordlist, and DPAPI chains where Chrome logins were decrypted automatically after a domain backup key was retrieved. A beacon object file also collects registry keys so services can be modeled.

The speakers argue that keeping raw data lets teams re-run newly discovered analysis on old engagements, work from an offline model of a network, and give every operator a new technique once it is added. Their takeaway is that structured, retained offensive data supports analytics and research. The project is open source on GitHub.

talks.summary:
Morgan Thomas, a cyber security engineer who moved into satellite security, aims this talk at security practitioners new to space. It starts by defining space as anything above the atmosphere and explains that a satellite pairs a ground station with an orbiting vehicle that can only be reached during passes overhead. The speaker compares this to the earlier spread of SCADA and IoT, since satellites must be small and resource-limited yet remain complex systems.

Next the talk covers the legal and ecosystem landscape. Five international heritage space laws date mostly from the 1960s and 1970s, and the cyber security standards issued between 2012 and 2023 guide development without being binding rules. Space is presented as a borderless, constantly changing attack surface, with an estimated 11,330 satellites from at least 92 countries in orbit by the end of 2022, and universities and startups increasingly involved. The speaker then outlines the satellite attack surface across flight compute, payloads, encryption and signals, noting operating systems such as VxWorks, openOS and Linux.

The threat section reviews suspected espionage groups, Turla's abuse of satellite communications to hijack downstream links, and recent incidents: an intrusion at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory through an unauthorized Raspberry Pi, a European Space Agency breach that exposed user data through a SQL flaw, and the AcidRain wiper. The speaker notes that documented attacks so far entered through ground stations rather than directly onto satellites, while a Department of Defense satellite hacking competition let teams run code on a live satellite. The talk closes with mapping resources, including the Sparta and TX frameworks, Space ISAC, and the competition's published papers.

talks.teaser: Seven practical lessons from running penetration tests against a large enterprise, from asset exposure to culture and certification.

The presentation frames seven lessons for building and running an internal penetration testing program at a large financial institution, using Sun Tzu’s “know yourself and know your enemy” as the opening theme. The first lessons stress mapping what the organization actually exposes: shadow IT websites, open S3 buckets discovered with public search tools, Shodan-style internet exposure, and the risk of forgotten externally hosted systems. It also covers thinking like attackers—credential stuffing on weaker portals, password spraying, and push-notification MFA fatigue—rather than assuming the perimeter alone defines risk.

Middle sections focus on assume-breach testing inside the network. Examples include unauthenticated Elasticsearch indexes that allowed large data dumps, Cisco Smart Install left enabled so switch configs and password hashes could be pulled, default password patterns shared across dozens of accounts, domain users as local administrators, secrets in GitHub and file shares, and pass-the-hash escalation. A separate thread explores curiosity in testing, including voice biometrics defeated by pitch-shifted recordings and spliced audio reminiscent of the film Sneakers.

Later lessons address organizational reality: certifications that satisfy PCI auditors and management (GPEN versus long experience without credentials), starting small and outsourcing gaps while growing a team, hiring curious testers, and shifting security left so developers embed secure practices before rushed pre-production tests. The close recaps all seven lessons and invites questions on remediation work the team performs after findings.

talks.teaser: Introduces Zeek's network analysis framework, its logs, scripting model and distributed design for newcomers.
talks.summary:
Zeek is presented as a network monitoring and deep packet inspection engine, formerly known as Bro, that has been in use for decades. Packets from a packet source pass through more than 70 protocol parsers, including several industrial protocol parsers, and then into an event engine with over 500 event types. The talk is pitched as a 101 introduction, so the speaker concentrates on core concepts for people who are new to the tool.

The session then moves into Zeek's scripting language, a procedural, strongly typed domain-specific language in which handlers receive connection records keyed by a four-tuple. A short example collects originating hosts from established connections into a set and prints them once a pcap has been processed. The speaker also covers the logging framework: the conn log, service logs tied together by a unique uid, the weird log for non-standard traffic, and the history field, which shows connections that never completed. The distributed design of workers, proxies and a manager is explained, with scaling possible both vertically and horizontally.

The closing section looks at use cases. One is Community ID correlation, which lets analysts pivot between endpoint detection data and network activity. Another is a Black Hat case in which multicast DNS traffic crossed network segments because of an undocumented default on vendor equipment, something the team caught early through Zeek logs rather than packet captures. The speaker points attendees to the package ecosystem, sample pcaps on zeek.org, and the community channels for feedback.

talks.teaser: Explains how threat intelligence can direct detection, hunting, red-team emulation, and remediation as one coordinated defense program.
talks.summary:
Security operations teams often drown in overlapping frameworks, vendor threat reports, and thousands of tracked actors and vulnerabilities, while intelligence is mistaken for raw feeds, news reading, or isolated IOC lists. The speaker frames a fusion center or SOC as an orchestra where incident response is the music and threat intelligence should conduct—turning aggregated, contextual information into decisions at tactical, operational, and strategic levels.

The middle of the talk introduces MITRE’s threat-informed defense model and its principles: stay dynamic and proactive, drive choices with intelligence, collaborate inside and outside the organization, keep analysis contextual to industry and risk appetite, and improve continuously. Starting from current resources, defenders build a organizational threat landscape, identify relevant adversaries and how they behave, and map techniques—often beginning with spreadsheets before using ATT&CK and Navigator. Combining overlapping TTPs yields choke points where controls may catch multiple actors. A worked example ties an APT28-style profile to detection for credential dumping, hunting for tooling, red-team emulation, prioritized vulnerability management, purple-team validation, and optional deception lures.

Practitioners should organize recurring time for intel, detection, and testing whether solo or as a team, make outcomes visible to leadership, and keep threat models accurate while watching for new and opportunistic attackers. The talk closes on maturing from external intelligence consumption toward internal mining and automation so cross-functional work produces measurable defenses rather than disconnected noise.

talks.title: 2023 - Matt Lorimer (zodiak) - TTX: (Probably) Not as Boring as They Sound
talks.teaser: Explains incident response tabletop exercises, from formal government-style drills to the casual Back Doors and Breaches card game.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case for tabletop exercises as a low-stress way to practise incident response. The speaker has seen organizations in the middle of a real incident that were unfamiliar with their own response plan, cyber insurance terms and team skills, and says those gaps are nearly impossible to work out mid-crisis. A tabletop lets a group walk through a scenario, expose weak spots and improve communication beforehand.

The formal route follows a federal tabletop package: scoping logistics and plausible scenarios with leadership, sending participants a handbook beforehand, running a facilitated session of one to ten scenarios, then closing with an after-action report and a brief hot wash while lessons are fresh. Facilitators feed information one data point at a time, data collectors take notes, players take action and observers stay passive. The speaker urges inviting analysts, responders and operations staff. Expected benefits include surfacing risks leadership never funded, such as missing email security, aligning inconsistent responses and building cross-team relationships.

For a casual option, the speaker covers Back Doors and Breaches, a card game from Black Hills Information Security. Hidden attack cards cover initial compromise, pivot, persistence, and command and control with exfiltration, while procedure cards add modifiers to d20 rolls. Failed rolls disable procedures and inject cards add complications. The speaker argues the exercise should not end until the team has traced the full intrusion, not just cleaned the infected machine. Running it with leadership first can turn executives into advocates.

talks.title: 2023 - Sherri Davidoff
talks.teaser: Zero-Day investigates 2023 - Sherri Davidoff.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Sherri Davidoff (CEO of LMG Security) explores the rising prevalence of mass zero-day exploits and supply chain attacks. Combining lessons from incidents such as MOVEit, SolarWinds, Log4j, Accellion, GoAnywhere, Kaseya, and Cisco IOS XE, Davidoff emphasizes that organizations must fundamentally assume compromise and vulnerability. The presentation outlines the mechanics of zero-day exploitation, the compounding risks introduced by third- and fourth-party technology vendors, and a structured response framework for handling zero-day disclosures.

### Key Topics
- **Targeting Sensitive Software & File Transfer Solutions:** Attackers intentionally target systems designed to hold or process sensitive data—notably secure file transfer appliances such as MOVEit Transfer, Accellion FTA, and GoAnywhere MFT. For example, the Clop ransomware gang weaponized zero-days against these platforms to steal sensitive data from thousands of victim organizations without needing to immediately notify or negotiate with each victim manually.
- **Holiday & Weekend Attack Timing:** Attackers frequently launch exploits during off-hours, weekends, or major holidays (e.g., the MOVEit campaign over Memorial Day weekend, Kaseya over the 4th of July). Mandiant/FireEye data highlights that 76% of ransomware attacks initiate after hours or on weekends, exposing organizations that lack 24/7 vulnerability intelligence monitoring.
- **Supply Chain Ripple Effects & Cascading Delays:** Exploitations of vendors (such as Fiserv or PwC using MOVEit) ripple downstream to clients like Flagstar Bank months after the original incident. Downstream organizations face delayed breach disclosures and complex investigations as each link in the supply chain assesses its exposure.
- **Root Causes of Zero-Day Proliferation:** Years of corporate source code thefts (e.g., Operation Aurora) and hacked bug-tracking databases (such as Microsoft's 2013 bug tracker breach reported in 2017) provide adversaries with proprietary blueprints to comb for unpatched flaws. Furthermore, mature zero-day exploit markets (e.g., 0day.today) now sell or freely distribute turnkey exploits.
- **Data Minimization as Primary Risk Reduction:** Because data hoarding drastically escalates breach liability (with average U.S. breach costs reaching $9.48 million according to IBM), organizations must implement automatic data retention and purging policies for temporary transfer systems, alongside maintaining rigorous hardware, software, and data inventories.

### Technical Details
- **The Cisco IOS XE Zero-Day Chain:** On October 16, Cisco announced a critical CVSS 10.0 vulnerability allowing remote attackers to execute level 15 admin commands and create a local user to access the web UI. Four days later (October 20), Cisco revealed a second vulnerability: a privilege escalation flaw enabling attackers to break out of IOS into underlying Linux, run arbitrary commands, and install a persistent implant/backdoor that survives local user remediation. Device telemetry tracked over 40,000 compromised devices until attackers altered their implant to return different HTTP responses (initially returning a 404), temporarily evading detection scripts.
- **Exploit & Detection Windows:** Attackers begin scanning within 15 minutes of public disclosure, and in cases like Log4j, weaponized exploits were observed in the wild a full day prior to public announcement. Conversely, Microsoft research shows it takes an average of 120 days (4 months) for newly patched vulnerabilities to be integrated into common automated vulnerability scanning tools.
- **Forensic Investigation Realities:** In a real-world response to a MobileIron server vulnerable to Log4j, LMG Security identified two distinct botnets (the Muhstik cryptojacking botnet and the Mirai DDoS botnet) co-existing on the same system. This aligns with Mandiant data showing multiple threat actors present in 27% of compromised environments.

### Takeaways
Organizations must treat zero-day disclosures as active security incidents rather than standard patching routines, executing a structured response checklist:
1. **Monitor Threat Intelligence 24/7:** Establish monitoring for vendor advisories and exploit intelligence across off-hours and holidays.
2. **Determine Applicability & Inventory:** Utilize software bills of materials (SBOMs) and accurate asset inventories to confirm running software and affected versions.
3. **Proactively Query Suppliers:** Mandate that key suppliers rapidly confirm whether they are running vulnerable software versions.
4. **Preserve Evidence Before Remediating:** Capture forensic images/logs prior to altering or rebuilding systems to preserve the ability to rule out data breaches for regulatory compliance.
5. **Enact Rapid Containment:** Minimize attack surfaces by disabling unnecessary public-facing web management interfaces (e.g., ports 80/443 on appliances or admin UIs).
6. **Hunt for Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) & Threats:** Patching alone does not remove previously planted implants, web shells, or secondary threat actors. Verify systems for compromise, monitor evolving IoC definitions, and perform deep threat hunting.
7. **Institutionalize Playbooks:** Adopt formal playbooks, such as CISA's Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks, and conduct regular incident response testing.

talks.title: 2023 - Andrew Brandt (spike)- You're No George Clooney...
talks.teaser: Two case studies show how plain personas and baroque delivery chains beat small firms while the payloads stayed commodity.
talks.summary:
The speaker recounts two early-year investigations where social engineering stayed deliberately low-key while malware staging grew bizarrely complex. The first wave hit tiny tax-preparation shops after a benign-looking client inquiry; only in the reply did the sender share a zip posing as prior returns. Decoy image and PDF extensions, an MP3 masquerading as documents, and a shortcut with an empty target field launched concealed PowerShell. Downloads rode legacy dotless and mixed hex-decimal IPv4 forms over HTTP, then roughly 200k of obfuscated Visual Basic that parked Guloader pieces in the registry for fileless persistence via hijacked Internet Explorer utilities.

The second case centered on a Swiss office duped by a fluent German caller posing as an urgent courier. While still on the line, the employee received a French shipping message whose entire body was one hot-linked image, chaining through a legitimate ad redirect to fake carrier sites. Opening the tracking app dropped trojanized portable Notepad++ whose license file hid nested PowerShell, impostor Comodo roots for Windows and Firefox, Tor with socat, and profiling aimed at finance and cryptocurrency sites. OSINT on shared artifacts linked parallel Electron delivery lures.

Practical lessons emphasize that helpful instincts beat Hollywood tradecraft for attackers, that warm paths into IT can halt incidents in minutes, and that unknown callers pushing email verification deserve the same doubt as sketchy attachments.

talks.teaser: Walks through the Flipper Zero's radios, NFC, RFID, infrared and firmware options, with live demos that partly failed.
talks.summary:
Troy Jessup gives a practical introduction to the Flipper Zero, a small handheld device that packs several radios and test tools into one case. He covers setup basics, including a microSD card with 16 GB suggested as the sweet spot and 64 GB as the stated maximum. He explains that the official firmware restricts some features, while community firmware such as Unleashed unlocks them, and he shows how the companion app handles configuration, updates and Bluetooth control.

The middle of the session tours the device's capabilities. A command-line chat feature failed during the live demo, so the speaker moved on. For NFC, he describes reading, writing and emulating 13.56 MHz tags, and a demo collected reader challenge responses from a lock so the keys could be cracked on a phone; the pairing step then failed. Guest expert Iceman explained the nonce-based mfkey32 approach for MIFARE Classic cards. Other topics include Amiibo emulation, GPIO prototyping, Ducky scripts, infrared remote replay, 125 kHz low-frequency RFID, and sub-GHz replay of garage and car key signals, where rolling codes make replay harder.

The closing portion surveys further apps and tools, then recommends trying custom firmware and the event's badge game before taking audience questions. The takeaway is that one inexpensive multi-tool can cover many radio and access-control experiments for people moving from basic to intermediate work.

talks.teaser: Walks through the RFID hacking toolkit, from Proxmark and Flipper Zero to cloners and relay attacks on access cards.
talks.summary:
Iceman gives a guided tour of RFID hacking, a field he says reaches far beyond door access control to transit tickets, vending machines, payment cards and phone emulation. He walks through the hardware a practitioner is likely to meet, including several Proxmark generations, the Flipper Zero with an HID SAM add-on, Chameleon Ultra emulators, cloners, field detectors and disruptive devices. For each, he explains what it does and when it is useful.

The middle of the talk covers techniques. Static nested nonces on some Mifare Classic clones defeat the usual nested-nonce key recovery, while key diversification functions let a card be dumped in seconds without breaking its crypto. Magic cards that change UIDs or use shadow mode are described as a cat-and-mouse game. Demonstrations include collecting data from a SEOS card with a Flipper and a SAM, and an iCLASS Elite key recovery from a dictionary. Relay attacks on SEOS doors, NDEF parsing and EMV terminals are discussed as prior research, and tearing attacks on EEPROM writes are presented as a deeper area.

He closes with practical advice: know your magic cards, be wary of cloud-based cloners that upload credential data to remote servers, and treat unverified offers for upgraded cloners with suspicion. He points listeners to a community list of RFID talks, the Proxmark forum file archive and an RFID hacking Discord for learning more.

talks.title: Wednesday Introduction
talks.summary:
### Overview
This session features conference announcements and updates regarding the event's interactive electronic badge and badge game. The speaker addresses ongoing battery drain issues experienced by attendees, invites the creator/voice behind the in-game character "Clippy" onto the stage to share gameplay statistics, provides instructions on acquiring game equipment, and introduces the community member facilitating the keynote presentation.

### Key Topics
- **Electronic Badge Power Issues:** Attendees are experiencing significant battery drain when attaching multiple mini badges. While the mini badges continue to illuminate or function, the voltage drops too low to power the main ESP module. Recommended mitigations include refreshing double-A batteries or utilizing the top plug with a portable battery pack while toggling the power switch.
- **Badge Game Engagement and Statistics:** A guest representing "Clippy" discusses attendee engagement, highlighting players camping outside the venue at 3:00 a.m. to access Wi-Fi bleeding onto the sidewalk to grind battles. The session provides specific gameplay metrics tracking player progress and outcomes.
- **Origin of Clippy:** The character originated as an internal joke modeled after Clippy the paperclip, which was later adapted with a 'K' by Chris.
- **Game Progression and Vending Machine Logistics:** Attendees are encouraged to complete their initial training and retrieve equipment packs from the venue vending machine. In cases where the vending machine is finicky, the Badge Life team distributes equipment manually upon presentation of a player code.

### Technical Details
- **Hardware Architecture:** The conference badge runs on an ESP module and operates on standard double-A batteries or an external plug input. Running numerous add-on mini badges creates an undervoltage condition where the peripheral mini badges function while the primary ESP module fails to boot or run.
- **Game Telemetry and Statistics:**
  - Characters joined: 1,144
  - Battles conducted: 2,727
  - Parties formed: 441
  - In-game burnouts: 928
  - Character deaths: 275

### Takeaways
Attendees should monitor badge power levels using external battery packs when running multiple mini badges, complete in-game training to acquire equipment packs, and consult the Badge Life area if automated vending fails. The session concludes with the introduction of community member Griff to present the keynote.

In this short hallway interview recorded at SaintCon, the conversation moves from the speaker's handle to his experience in hacker culture and conferences. Bill Swearingen explains that he picked his handle in the early 1990s while running a piracy-focused bulletin board system, and that the name came from a virus he made by clicking through a virus generator tool. He says he prefers smaller gatherings, where people can meet like-minded attendees and still spend real time together, and contrasts that with the more corporate feel he finds at larger events.

He then describes a favourite past project from around 2001 or 2002: a device that triggered preemption on traffic signals so the lights turned green. He and a friend tested it while driving around Kansas City, and the work drew press coverage. He also recalls a talk on police radar and laser countermeasures, which surveyed the laws in different states about jamming and detection. On incident response, he says the recent cases he has handled were mostly straightforward domain admin compromises, and that persistent threats now look more like hacking by numbers than advanced techniques.

The conversation closes with community and travel. He mentions a monthly Kansas City group that meets on the second Tuesday of the month, and his habit of introducing himself to people sitting alone at its events. The main takeaway is about connection: approach people, and smaller events make that easier. The chat is light and personal rather than technical.

Brandon says he works as a network security engineer and describes a childhood drawn to computers, when he would step in to help classmates with their machines even after a teacher teased him for it. He recalls the monochrome Apple II machines of that era, with their dual five-and-a-quarter-inch floppy drives and built-in keyboards.

The conversation then moves to a lighthearted segment. The host quizzes Brandon on Gen Z slang, which he mostly does not recognise, and the two trade jokes about odd hypotheticals, such as having boulder-sized hands and what advantages they might bring. Brandon jokes that such hands would probably keep him out of karate tournaments.

To close, Brandon says he has enjoyed the talks and the chance to socialise at the event. He notes that the conference feels comfortable for introverts because people here are genuinely interested in technical discussion rather than tolerating it. The clip is informal and offers no technical instruction, so it mainly gives a sense of how one practitioner came to the field and how the event felt to him.

A Saint Con hallway segment features Caleb Smith, who goes by cleeb online, tracing his handle to high school friends misreading “Caleb” and later shortening it further in college. He describes attending his second Saint Con after shifting from general IT and sysadmin work toward information security a few months before his first visit.

He recalls placing seventh in last year’s hackers challenge, a result that convinced him he could land an infosec role; he now works in the field for Nemus. When asked for a single defensive tool, he picks Wireshark after a mentor from the home labs community walked him through a packet capture CTF in about an hour. The interviewer contrasts Zeek and Suricata for fast metadata-driven answers before deeper Wireshark work, and both argue that skilled staff outweigh flashy appliances, with open source as the sensible starting point until scale demands commercial products.

The conversation turns personal: Caleb holds an extra-class amateur radio license, mentors younger hams online, and enjoys retro computing trivia. He advises his younger self to stop stressing about being good enough, and tells his future self to appreciate what he already has instead of chasing every new shiny stack.

The segment opens with a first-time SAINTCON attendee comparing the event to larger cons and praising downstairs villages, hands-on challenges, and the chance to learn techniques in person rather than only from recorded talks. The guest reflects on delivering a talk drawn from personal experience, including nerves despite a calm stage presence, and a style of using sparse picture cues instead of dense speaker notes.

She describes the talk’s theme as contrasting marketed security-career expectations with day-to-day reality, and notes audience members—especially newcomers—said it eased imposter syndrome. The exchange turns to burnout, mental health in high-stress roles, and a long-term idea of training as a therapist after leaving technology. She outlines current work as vice president of a WiCyS neurodiversity affiliate, advocating accommodations such as dim lighting, and shares a late diagnosis journey plus relatable LinkedIn Learning modules on social engineering and phishing.

Closing threads cover how she pivoted from journalism into information assurance after discovering the major in college, why curiosity kept her in the field, weighing DevSecOps versus management, and learning from managers who struggle to delegate. She favors staying hands-on enough to move between IC and leadership rather than treating either path as irreversible.

Saint Con highlights include The Vault challenge—physical breaking and entering that stayed fun even after pants tore and first place slipped when others used molded fingerprints on the safe. The chat closes with rock climbing as stress relief, fatigue with Cards Against Humanity, and a light solar-flare scenario about work without computers.

Training later grew into a company, and the Core Group training merged into Red Team Alliance. During the pandemic, when classes moved online, the team built a compact enclosure with a full access control system inside, which remote students kept on their desks. It can switch to a debug mode that exposes card data, and students could see whether a badge read succeeded.

The conversation then moves to lighter subjects: an airplane-themed talk that used a mock drinks cart, favorite travel spots such as Norway and Vietnam, and a wish list that includes Iceland, Antarctica and Alaska. The main takeaway is how unplanned opportunities and flexibility turned into a career, and how a constraint like remote teaching produced a useful teaching tool.

This hallway interview at SAINTCON starts with JC, who runs the Vault challenge at the conference. This year the Vault was rebuilt from the ground up using lessons from earlier years. The safe-cracking element drew heavy interest, and although the instructions run several pages, people were able to work through them. One first-time attendee spent two hours on it and opened most of a safe.

JC then traces his path into security. He left high school for an IT job, moved into classified network support as an information system security officer in San Diego, and was drawn to incident response after a SANS course. Later he worked on PCI investigations and then ran his own firm, which now handles penetration testing, incident response and malware analysis. For the Vault, the first year's challenges were all solved easily, so the second year added a weighted idol wired to an Arduino that set off an alarm when the weight changed too quickly. A team defeated it with a bag of chickpeas, and later designs used commercial door hardware instead.

JC's favourite exploit came from reverse engineering a large keylogger malware family, where weak encoding of an FTP password let him reach the operators' server and the victims' data. That access raised ethical questions about what to do with it. The interview closes on lighter topics: a favourite N64 Zelda game, and plans to someday open a breakfast-style food truck or a fine-dining restaurant, possibly after culinary school. JC's wish for the rest of the conference is simply to relax, with a calmer team atmosphere this year.

In this casual hallway interview at SAINTCON, the guest known as Sticks explains where the handle came from and reflects on his long history with the conference. He first attended a Utah edition around 2001 at the Eccles Broadcast Center, ran audio at Weber State many years ago, and has stayed on the AV crew since.

The conversation then turns to music. He has played drums since childhood and wrote songs on guitar with former bandmates, but has mostly worked solo since his last band fell apart during the pandemic. He currently collaborates with a guitarist who handles arrangements while he writes lyrics and records vocals. His favorite conference memory is bringing his daughter, who was getting interested in technology, to an event where the two worked through hacker challenges and soldered badges together.

He also recounts a story from his work at UEN, where he helped schools defend against students getting around their security controls. He was once one of those students, bypassing filters to play video games. He traces the evolution of content filtering there, from a filter that ran on a caching server to a purpose-built appliance, and describes how multi-site web servers caused legitimate sites to be blocked or harmful ones to slip through. The exchange ends on a light note: a student who gets around today's controls may one day be the one being interviewed.

They describe growing up curious about computers, sparked partly by a ReBoot episode that mentioned hidden file attributes, and a pattern of pushing curiosity far enough to get in trouble.

A standout school-era story involved Pegasus Mail: a filter that bounced messages with semicolons in the To field fivefold, which a friend duplicated and accidentally amplified into thousands of messages until the campus mail system failed and accounts were locked. On the conference side, they recall badge work beginning around BSides Salt Lake City after PCB hobby attempts, drawing inspiration from prior badge makers, and treating the first successful design as rare compared with later experiments.

They contrast favorite badges for challenge value versus aesthetics, including Defcon games and a black-badge win aided when post-COVID remote badge shipments leaked chip and firmware hints before in-person diffs. They close by favoring Montreal for the conference crowd over sightseeing, a light personal anecdote, and thanks for the visit.

talks.title: Hallway
talks.teaser: Hallway chat delivers a St. George power pentest, police detention, FOIA body-cam footage, and millennial tech trivia.
talks.summary:
The segment opens as an informal hallway conversation at a security conference. The guest describes an April physical penetration test for a power company in St. George: the team reached the server room, crossed a drop ceiling into a restricted area, and left to find police reviewing camera footage. An responding officer drew a weapon and ordered them to the ground; they were detained, verified against the engagement, and released after client contacts confirmed their role.

The guest describes obtaining multiple officers’ body-worn camera recordings through a public records request and plans to sync that footage with themed shirt imagery. They reflect on whether clients should pre-notify law enforcement—helpful for safety but potentially skewing response-time metrics—and note a keynote prompt about who in the room has been detained. The interviewer pivots to a millennial-era technology quiz (MySpace, DB-9, AltaVista, Netscape, RJ-11, Napster, LaserDisc) and light personal questions.

### Overview
This interview takes place in the hallway at SAINTCON in Provo, where the host interviews Clint (also referred to by the handle atticus88). Clint reflects on his long history with the conference, beginning with his first attendance in 2014 at Weber State, his multi-year involvement with building conference badges, and his ongoing role mentoring attendees in the Hardware Hacking Village.

### Key Topics
- **SAINTCON Origins and First Attendance:** Clint discusses attending his first SAINTCON in 2014 at Weber State, which coincided with the host's first year as well.
- **Badge Engineering and Volunteering:** Clint describes how he got commandeered by Luke into contributing to the conference badge in 2014 by writing software, ultimately helping build badges for around four years.
- **Hardware Hacking Village:** After stepping back from the intensive badge-building process, Clint transitioned to volunteering in the Hardware Hacking Village, assisting participants with soldering and hardware projects.
- **Conference Challenges and Activities:** Clint shares his favorite events to watch and join, including tamper-evident tape contests, default challenges, and escape-and-evasion style challenges such as escaping zip ties.
- **Handle Origin:** Clint reveals the story behind his handle, `atticus88`, explaining that it combines his birth year with his favorite character from *To Kill a Mockingbird*.

### Technical Details
- **Badge Features:** Clint worked on badge software development over roughly four years. His favorite project was the second badge he worked on, designed like a gamepad, where he incorporated map rendering and localization software to pinpoint attendee locations (the "parking lot GPS").
- **Hardware Village Safety & Soldering:** In the Hardware Hacking Village, Clint helps attendees solder. He notes that while soldering burns and minor injuries happen commonly—mentioning he burned himself in his hotel room and caught a bag on fire the previous night—serious blister-causing burns have been rare, with only about one severe incident involving a younger participant.

### Takeaways
- Community-driven efforts like badge creation often start on a whim ("we could do a thing") and require hundreds of hours of volunteer software and hardware development.
- Transitioning from high-intensity badge engineering to the Hardware Hacking Village allows experienced makers to mentor new attendees and share soldering skills in a hands-on environment.
- Interactive spectator and participatory challenges like tamper-evident and restraint escapes highlight the culture and hands-on learning at hacker conferences.

Assembly time varies between hot-swap and solder builds, with mounting style and microcontroller choice affecting difficulty and price.

Listeners hear switch families (linear, tactile, clicky), lubing for feel, keycap profiles and clone debates, and reputable off-the-shelf brands versus problematic retail experiences. Several built boards are shown as examples of themed and daily-driver setups, and storefront links are promised for profiles, parts, and trusted vendors.

talks.title: metacortex - Password Attacks From Ashigaru to Daimyo
talks.teaser: Walks through password hashing, cracking methods like brute force, wordlists, rules and masks, and GPU-based hashcat runs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why passwords matter: compromising one credential can expose everything that account reaches, and users often choose weak ones. It explains how hashing turns input into a fixed-length digest, shown with a short Python demo where the same input always gives the same SHA-256 output but a one-character change alters it completely. Comparing hashes rather than stored plaintext is presented as the basic defence.

The middle section covers the main cracking approaches. Brute force tries every combination and is thorough but can become impractical as length grows. Wordlists are fast but only succeed if the password appears in the list, and hybrid attacks add digits to dictionary words. Rules apply substitutions and mutations to wordlist entries. Rainbow tables are described as largely obsolete because of their storage size. Salting is covered as a defence, since unique per-entry salts make attacks much harder. Demos compare simple Python brute-force and wordlist scripts with hashcat attack modes, masks and rule files.

The closing part explains cracking time as total possibilities divided by guesses per second, and how CUDA-enabled GPUs have raised that rate, so password policies must keep pace with hardware. The speaker describes a GPU cracking rig used in audits and cautions against submitting sensitive hashes to online cracking services. The takeaway is to require longer passwords, use salted hashes and audit for predictable organisational patterns.

talks.title: Andrew Goble and Panel - "Ouch, That Hurt!" or Lessons Learned over a Decade of Pentests
talks.teaser: Higher-ed security staff share a decade of consortium pentest stories, from a runaway printer to physical intrusions.
talks.summary:
A panel of security staff from several Utah higher-education institutions looks back on roughly a decade of penetration tests run across their consortium. The program began in the mid-2000s when university CIOs, worried about weak networks, commissioned an ad hoc team. It later settled into a funded model in which the team visits four institutions each fiscal year, roughly every two years per school. Early on, the speakers say, the assessments met suspicion, and the team often found low-hanging fruit such as unlocked machines and open doors.

The stories show how the work changed. One early network scan sent a registrar's printer into a loop, wasting transcript paper and causing lasting friction, which led to much better communication with each school before testing. Physical tests exposed weak controls around a data center and a lock shop that was also an IT system, and one blind test drew a police response after hours. Over time, schools adopted network segmentation and blocked SMB traffic across their networks, and engagement moved toward purple-team collaboration, where defenders and testers work through detections together.

The panel's takeaways are that end users and social engineering remain the easiest way in, that asset inventory and old vulnerabilities are persistent gaps, and that Active Directory weaknesses keep recurring. They recommend securing leadership buy-in and stable funding, sharing lessons across institutions, and building an internal assessment team, since insiders understand where the real risk sits.

She describes SAINTCON as a yearly stop for the class, with soldering and the team hacker challenge among the activities students enjoy.

The middle of the talk covers CyberPatriot, a national competition run by the U.S. Air Force Association with thousands of teams of up to six people. Students get training through Cisco Networking Academy, which provides virtual machines and Linux tutorials. In the state round, teams work through four downloaded images, which can include Windows 10, a Windows Server version from 2008 to 2019, and Ubuntu. They also solve a Packet Tracer networking problem and answer a quiz of about 30 questions, and the scores are combined and compared with other teams in the state. The top 13 teams nationally advance to the national finals, which moved to a virtual format last year.

Yocom explains the classroom preparation, including a dry run to whitelist the tools teams need, such as Discord, so they work on the school network. Team members then share what they value about SAINTCON and CyberPatriot, including the forensic questions, the hacker challenge and working with friends. The takeaway is that a hands-on, team-based approach lets students build practical skills while they compete.
