talks.title: Bart Stump - "Just Scraping By" - The Privacy Implications of Mining the Internet
talks.teaser: Walks through public mugshot, social-media and state-record cases to show how easily personal data resurfaces online.
talks.summary:
Bart Stump opens by arguing that people should assume there is no real privacy on the internet and that anything posted can resurface years later. He illustrates this with several cases: an executive's emails from about eleven years earlier that came up in a workplace investigation, a top-ranked football draft prospect whose stock fell after a video from his own social account was posted the night before the draft, and a communications director whose offhand post during a flight became a worldwide trend before she was fired.

The talk then covers the project that grew out of these examples. It began as a web-scraping experiment on public jail booking photos. The speaker describes recent Utah legislation that restricted publish-for-pay mugshot sites while still letting media and others request the records. He also reviews tools he tried, including Octoparse for scraping and Maltego for social media transforms, and notes that some of the social media features were costly or required subscriptions.

The main idea, called CancelBot, was described as a tool where a name, email address or phone number would return public profiles and posts that could be searched by keyword, so people can review their own public footprint. Related ideas included helping people spot exploitation-related search terms and giving parents and teenagers guidance on what their public presence shows. The takeaway is to assume published material is permanent and to check what is publicly visible about yourself.

talks.title: Waylon Grange - 1 21 GigaWatts!
talks.teaser: Shows how a residential solar panel controller falls to hardware access, firmware decryption and hard-coded passwords.
talks.summary:
The talk documents a hardware and firmware assessment of a home solar panel gateway, starting with the vendor's consumer and installer mobile apps. Both were .NET wrappers, and decompiling them exposed a public cloud storage bucket of firmware packages plus an index mapping images to devices. The packages were encrypted, and the decryption tool was only available inside the firmware, so the researcher needed a way onto the device first. A native routine in the installer app turned out to derive the installer password from the username and serial number.

On the hardware side, the controller exposed a UART console while JTAG was disabled, and the kernel rejected input over the serial line. Glitching the root filesystem failed because the device panicked on tampering. Instead, the researcher dumped the external boot flash with a hardware programmer, changed one byte in the U-Boot environment to restore a boot delay, and reflashed the chip. That gave a U-Boot prompt, from which the filesystem could be read and the decryption tool recovered. The decryption key was derived from hashed string blocks in the binary, so the firmware could be decrypted. A web upgrade function then allowed unsanitized command execution on the box.

Root login still failed because a custom PAM module ignored the shadow file and checked a hard-coded, serial-derived password instead. Three CVEs traced back to that module, and owners could not change the password. A later firmware change added firewall rules but also a URL that disabled them shortly after boot. The talk closes by noting that serial numbers are printed on the case and labels, so these credentials are predictable. The takeaways are to avoid hard-coded passwords, never roll your own crypto, and fail hard when hardware has been tampered with.

talks.title: Bryce Fox
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate Bryce Fox and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
Bryce Fox, an Enterprise IT Architect at the University of Utah with 30+ years in IT, delivered 'Networking 101,' an introductory talk on fundamental networking concepts for beginners. The session covered the evolution of Local Area Networks (LANs) from bus topologies using hubs to modern star topologies with switches. Fox explained how switches reduced collision domains to just the wire between the switch and host, improving network efficiency. He detailed MAC addressing and the ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) protocol for device discovery within LANs, explaining that MAC addresses are identified by manufacturer through the first three hexadecimal digits.

The talk introduced VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) as a way to segment networks virtually on physical switches, and VLAN tagging (IEEE 802.1Q) for carrying multiple VLANs across interconnected switches. Fox presented the OSI seven-layer model—Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application—and contrasted it with the practical TCP/IP model, which consolidates the upper layers into software-handled functions.

Fox provided detailed instruction on IPv4 addressing, including how octets work in binary and decimal (0-255), subnet masks for defining network boundaries, and the evolution from classful networking (Class A, B, C with fixed masks) to Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) using slash notation (e.g., /27). He compared TCP (connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, with handshaking) and UDP (connectionless, fast, lossy, without handshaking). Additional topics included DNS for name-to-IP translation, routing between networks, and practical use of ARIN (American Registry for Internet Numbers) to look up IP address ownership and network registration. The speaker emphasized this was foundational material and directed experienced attendees to advanced talks such as Wireshark packet analysis.

talks.title: Kyle Feuz - Wireshark : A Beginners Introduction
talks.teaser: Walks beginners through Wireshark's interface, capture placement, baselining, TLS decryption, filters and Nmap scan detection.
talks.summary:
This two-hour beginner training introduces Wireshark through hands-on work with prepared capture files, avoiding live captures and the legal questions they raise. The session tours the packet list, packet details and packet bytes panes, then covers where to capture traffic. The right capture point depends on the traffic of interest, and the speaker covers switch port mirroring, network taps and the challenges of wireless capture.

The middle section focuses on baselining normal traffic so anomalies stand out. Attendees compare a baseline capture with others using capture file properties, protocol hierarchy and endpoint statistics. For encrypted web traffic, the speaker shows how to set the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable so a browser writes TLS session keys, then loads that file into Wireshark to decrypt HTTP, follow streams and export transferred objects.

The final part covers efficiency through custom profiles, display filters, filter buttons and coloring rules. A default Nmap scan serves as the case study: a sequential ARP sweep finds active hosts, then one source sends a burst of SYN attempts across many ports, producing reset packets. The takeaway is to learn what normal looks like on your own network before hunting for deviations.

talks.title: Matt Lorimer and Panel - Why climb the corporate ladder when hacking the elevator is more fun?
talks.teaser: A panel of Utah security leaders answers audience questions on career moves, burnout, mentorship, and landing jobs in infosec.
talks.summary:
The session frames infosec careers as deliberate growth rather than a straight climb up management. Matt Lorimer moderates a panel of practitioners and executives who take turns answering questions from the floor on when to leave a role, how culture and passion factor in, and what to do after a layoff.

Audience questions drive most of the material. Panelists discuss moving from a third-party SOC toward incident response through home labs, certifications, and curiosity; reducing burnout via mental health, boundaries, and work-life balance; elevating security leaders to executive and board conversations; balancing remote and in-office collaboration; impostor feelings versus self-doubt; networking through alumni outreach, conferences, and starting local groups; staying technical while leading; and roles that emphasize people contact such as customer success, compliance, and privacy. Hiring managers stress motivation, humility, and relevant extracurricular work over résumé filler.

The closing themes tie networking at events like SAINTCON to long-term opportunity and urge career changers to translate earlier field experience by showing initiative through labs, competitions, and projects that prove interest in security.

talks.summary:
The speaker introduces radio frequency as a broadcast medium that anyone in range can receive, and explains how software-defined radio lets a computer tune to and decode those signals. A basic receiver dongle costs around 40 dollars. The talk compares receivers such as the AirSpy with transmit-capable devices like the HackRF and YardStick One, and covers software including GNU Radio, SDR# and SDR++.

Practical examples follow. Antenna length is tied to wavelength, so a quarter-wave antenna suits 1090 MHz aircraft transponder reception, which the speaker used to map nearby flights. A public FCC ID printed on a utility power meter led to its operating band of 902 to 927 MHz, showing how device filings can reveal frequencies. Wireless utility meters and water treatment telemetry on unlicensed ISM bands were discussed as data that nearby listeners can capture. Attack categories covered eavesdropping, man-in-the-middle, replay and forged messages, with a replay weakness in a home security keypad from earlier research as an example.

The closing message is that encoding is not encryption, and that an inexpensive dongle and free software are enough to start exploring which nearby transmissions are unprotected. Attendees were pointed toward GNU Radio tutorials as a next step for decoding and replaying signals.

The speaker describes a storage server he built in a Supermicro chassis, buying six large drives at different retail stores and burning them in before installation, and he notes that enterprise surplus gear has become harder to find. He frames home lab planning around three factors, upfront hardware cost, ongoing power cost and performance, along with how much noise and clutter the household will tolerate.

Hardware options are compared by price and capability. Small thin clients and tiny desktops offer cheap compute for small clusters, while 1U servers offer more memory and out-of-band management. The speaker warns that a lower-TDP CPU can run hotter in a case with a low T-case limit, raising fan noise. Budget X99 motherboards from overseas marketplaces can host ECC or non-ECC memory in a desktop case. Networking covers used switches, with a caution that one switch rebooted when fed by a modified sine wave UPS, and host bus adapters need airflow to avoid errors.

The closing part covers hiding gear in a furniture build, separating production services from lab work by nesting a lab inside a bare-metal ESXi host behind a physical edge firewall, and choosing hypervisors such as ESXi, Proxmox or unRAID. Q&A closes the session.

talks.teaser: A defender-oriented walkthrough of modern ransomware tactics, extortion trends, and practical controls from backups to least privilege.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames ransomware as an end-to-end attack on organizations that want money, walking from reconnaissance and common initial access paths such as phishing, weak patching, and RDP password spraying through execution, persistence, privilege escalation, evasion, further discovery, lateral movement, and encryption impact. It then explains how defenders who rely on backups pushed attackers toward double extortion: collection, command and control, and exfiltration ahead of leak sites that prove stolen data and demand payment.

The middle surveys the scale and variety of the ecosystem, citing VirusTotal figures on submitted samples and families, RaaS and affiliate revenue splits, platform targets including Android and Mac, and newer pressure tactics such as data auctions, direct extortion of customers and third parties, and the coined term killware tied to patient harm when hospitals lose systems. Economic and policy context includes large payout examples, Atlanta’s recovery-versus-ransom tradeoff, proposed reporting rules, restrictions on paying designated terrorist groups, and the middlemen used to route payments.

The closing focuses on what practitioners can do: staffing and training, mapping behavior to MITRE ATT&CK, strong revision-controlled off-site backups, phased removal of local administrator rights and need-to-know file access, patching and compensating controls for unpatchable assets, segmentation, EDR/XDR, SIEM visibility, breach-assessment and atomic red-team validation, CISA guidance, red-team exercises that prove detection rather than checkbox compliance, IR retainers, and tabletop payment decisions. A brief Q&A touches Colonial Pipeline backlash, geo-based ransomware kill switches, insurance tightening, and security involvement in backup testing.

The speaker walks through the three implementation groups, which fit small businesses with little IT staff, organizations with dedicated IT and more complex operations, and mature organizations handling sensitive data. He highlights controls that are hard in practice, such as authorized software and libraries, data labeling, role-based access control, endpoint management, and anti-exploitation features. He argues that many of these are organizational problems more than technical ones, requiring work with HR and business leadership.

The closing discussion covers getting leadership buy-in, documenting accepted risk when management declines a control, and sequencing work by following the order of the controls within an implementation group. Attendees shared how they used asset coverage metrics to show leaders that controls were under-deployed and money was being wasted, and how an incident can open the door to funding. The talk ends with an invitation to follow one safeguard per day in a community Discord channel dedicated to the controls.

talks.title: Dys-FUNctional Cloud Red Teaming
talks.summary:
The talk explains how red teamers can use managed AWS services such as API Gateway, Lambda and CloudFormation to get offensive work done more efficiently. It covers serverless frameworks, including Zappa and the AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM), and how they fit into the console, control plane and data plane layers of a cloud provider.

The first use case is discovering AWS account IDs, a 12-digit number that vendors often share for cross-account features. A SAM-deployed Lambda generated random IDs and checked the sign-in URL response, where a 302 indicated a valid account; over an hour of scheduled runs it collected about 40 valid accounts. The second case uses the S3 expected bucket owner option: a known account ID can be tested against a publicly reachable resource to learn which account hosts it. The third is command and control, where API Gateway forwards callbacks to any server, so traffic looks like it goes to a trusted Amazon domain.

The final section covers disrupting CloudTrail logging in a compromised account. Deleting a trail and quickly recreating it with an attacker-owned S3 bucket can keep the delete event out of the defender's log pipeline, and a Lambda can scrub suspicious entries from logs. The main defence is to send logs to a separate, trusted AWS account so an attacker with access to one account cannot edit them.

talks.title: Badge Assembly

It opens with the kit contents: a lanyard, a paper sheet holding a gift code for designing a custom mini badge through OSH Park, mini badge holder boards, and a daughter board with the microcontroller. The main board gets surface-mount pads soldered to its edges, then eight red LEDs are seated with their flat sides and short cathode legs matched to the silkscreen. The LEDs are tested before the remaining parts go on.

Next, the battery holder is soldered to the back of the main board and the button is checked to cycle through the LED modes. The vertical and horizontal side boards slot into their notches, and the pads must line up or the part is reversed. A rubber band helps hold the ball structure steady while each joint is soldered. Seventeen mini badge holders are then snapped from their panel, four of which have a horizontal slot orientation. Headers go onto each holder before it is fitted to the ball, and the wider slot on each board keeps the orientation correct.

To finish, the presenter builds the year's mini badge, placing a surface-mount LED and resistor on its back. A powered-down badge serves as a jig to keep the pins straight while they are soldered. Spare parts in the kit cover the custom mini badge the builder designs. The practical takeaways are to test each subsystem early, check alignment before final soldering, and confirm LED polarity.

talks.title: 2019 - hamster - Getting Started with KiCAD (alternate)
talks.teaser: Shows how to design a mini badge PCB in KiCad, from artwork and schematic through to ordering boards.

The talk is a beginner-oriented walkthrough of designing a small "mini badge" circuit board in KiCad, an open-source PCB design tool. The speaker explains why the fixed, roughly one-inch form factor makes a good first project, since power and microcontroller concerns can be left out. The early part covers basic board vocabulary: vias, traces, copper pours, solder mask and silkscreen, along with two-layer stackups, surface finish options, and the units that fabricators use.

The middle section follows the workflow. Artwork should be drawn as vectors at one-to-one scale in a tool such as Illustrator or Inkscape, kept in black and white, and exported at high resolution so the KiCad importer keeps clean curves. The speaker recommends drawing a schematic first, associating footprints with parts, and solving the ratsnest by routing traces. Design rules should match the fabricator's minimum trace and space, around six to seven mils, and the design rules check should be run before exporting Gerber files, which are then verified in a viewer. Panelizing several designs on one sheet, and the cost trade-offs between low-cost overseas board houses and domestic ones, are also discussed. Parts sourcing from distributors and marketplaces comes up, along with hand assembly of surface-mount parts using solder paste and a griddle.

The closing part covers practical cautions: language barriers and shipping delays with overseas vendors, price breaks that encourage over-ordering, and the value of small prototype runs for checking colour matches before committing to a large batch. The main takeaway is that a first board is inexpensive to produce, and mistakes are a useful way to learn the process.

talks.title: 2019 - Popes - Hacking Hackers, Sure you can borrow my clicker!
talks.teaser: Explores keystroke injection into vulnerable wireless mice and keyboards using a cheap radio, plus the patching gaps behind it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's background in volunteering at security conferences and in a local DC 435 group. It then turns to a weakness in wireless input devices. The speaker had seen the 2016 MouseJack disclosure and later the 2019 clicker injection research, and set out to test it. Using a low-cost 2.4 GHz USB radio that can scan channels and pull out a device's address, the speaker describes an early home lab attempt to inject keystrokes into a Logitech receiver. The first several tries failed, and the speaker eventually found that the injected input was actually reaching their own keyboard and mouse.

The middle section covers field results. At a Black Hat knock team engagement, the speaker's radio picked up several nearby wireless keyboards and mice, and some of them accepted injected keystrokes. A similar result came up at the DEF CON Wall of Sheep. The speaker then walks through the patch situation: Logitech's 2016 fix was incomplete, a 2019 update had to be sought out by hand for unifying receivers, and some users reported that the update broke their devices. New hardware bought at retail was described as shipping unpatched, and non-unifying clickers cannot be patched at all. The speaker also built an Electron-based control app that sends keystrokes over the radio, runs a short PowerShell payload on Windows, and shows a chat-style interface that lets one person use another person's keyboard.

The closing part gives practical advice. Teams in sensitive roles should use wired peripherals, and presenters should use a dedicated laptop rather than their own machine. Receivers should be patched where possible, and unknown USB dongles should be treated as a risk. The speaker promised a follow-up walkthrough for building the setup and called for better patch delivery from vendors.

Scoring stays playful, with gag prizes and running commentary from the host.

The session closes by thanking organizers and everyone who presented or supplied decks, framing the hour as intentional comic relief near the end of the conference. talks.title: 2019 - Mike Julander - Intro to I2C on the Buspirate
talks.teaser: Introduces I2C basics and shows how a Bus Pirate reads and writes the EEPROM inside a conference badge.
talks.summary:
The talk is a hands-on introduction to I2C, a protocol where one master device talks to several addressed chips over a shared clock and data line. The speaker uses a conference badge as the example: a small EEPROM chip stores text that the badge shows on its screen, and each device answers to its own address and confirms with an acknowledgement bit.

The middle of the talk covers the Bus Pirate, a low-cost multi-protocol tool that works as an I2C interface and a basic logic analyzer. The speaker connects over a serial terminal, switches the device into I2C mode, and runs the built-in address search, which finds the chip at write address A0 in hex. He then explains the EEPROM's sequential read behavior, writes a short message to memory using a text-message flag and a length byte, and shows it appearing on the badge alongside the existing animations. A live attempt to sniff traffic from the badge did not work during the session.

In the questions, the speaker notes that the chip's address-changing options depend on configuration and lock bits, so he avoids them, and points attendees to the datasheet for anyone who wants to explore further. The takeaway is that the Bus Pirate lets a tester probe a bus interactively instead of writing custom microcontroller debug code for every experiment.

talks.teaser: Shows how a conference network was built and run on cloud-managed gear, covering Wi-Fi, switching, logging and troubleshooting.
talks.summary:
Tristan Rhodes, a network architect, explains how he built the network for a SAINTCON conference with about 1,200 attendees. The organizers wanted a fast internet link they fully controlled so attendee experiments would not be blocked, and they needed to fence off areas where hacking was expected. Badges stayed off Wi-Fi to avoid competing for airtime. The design used one gigabit link from a sponsoring ISP with about 30 public addresses, two firewalls, switches, and cameras spread across three floors and five closets joined by single-mode fiber.

The talk then tours cloud-managed Meraki features. A packet capture could be started on a client's switch port in a few clicks, and dedicated radios on the access points provided a spectrum view of channel use. Change logs, offline-device alerts, scheduled firmware upgrades with rollback, and a topology map helped a small volunteer team track changes. Layer 2 isolation protected servers, a separate SSID was made for a hacking training, and DHCP snooping blocked rogue DHCP offers. The speaker also listed drawbacks, including no IPv6 support, limited firewall rule design, and outbound NAT through a single address.

By Wednesday, about 1,280 devices had connected, with Apple the most common vendor and roughly 30 percent using randomized MAC addresses, which made device identification unreliable. Peak usage reached about 600 megabits per second, and about 34 percent of traffic was UDP, likely VPN or streaming. The main lessons were to enable DHCP snooping at the access layer and to plan monitoring and logging before the event starts.

### Overview
In this hallway-style conversation, Kevin Howard (known by the handle "Lean" or historically "Lean O'Malley") discusses his background, garage office setup, the origins and evolution of the SAINTCON conference, and pressing challenges regarding cybersecurity mentorship and community growth.

### Key Topics
- **Home Office "Bubble" Setup**: Kevin details building an enclosed plastic workspace inside his third-car garage while renovating his basement, incorporating portable AC venting, smart temperature automation, boom microphones with hardware mute buttons, multiple monitors, and a dedicated meeting display.
- **Origin of the Handle "Lean"**: Around age 12, feeling like the odd one out or an "anomaly," Kevin adapted the French phrase "l'anomalie" into "Lean O'Malley," which was later shortened to "Lean."
- **History and Evolution of SAINTCON**: Originally started as the Utah Education Network Security Summit to help state education and agency IT personnel exchange threat intelligence, the conference was built through grassroots volunteer efforts. Kevin got involved in his early twenties, initially attending a summit at Richfield or Snow, then volunteering and eventually writing a 40-page Nmap workbook for training in 2010. The name evolved from SAINT (Security Advisory and Incident Network Team) into SAINTCON, growing from roughly 60 people to a capped attendance of around 1,500.
- **Conference Challenges and Competitions**: Discussion touches on technical setup hurdles (such as VGA upscaling versus HDMI handshakes) and designing challenges like the Vault, Lockpicking, and Hackers Challenge. Kevin highlights the difficulty of creating challenges that push elite teams—such as a safe with a fingerprint scanner reverse-engineered over 36 hours—while keeping content approachable for beginners, especially as events pivot toward virtual formats.
- **Mentorship and Industry Career Pipeline**: The speakers examine the rapid growth of the infosec sector, issues surrounding negative unemployment, junior staff being placed under senior-level pressure, imposter syndrome, and community fragmentation. Kevin advocates for localized mentorship programs and guiding newcomers who are willing to put in the effort to learn.

### Technical Details
- **Early Attack Trends & Tools**: Mentions of early threat sharing covering SSH brute forcing, WEP cracking using Orinoco Gold PCMCIA cards, rainbow tables cracking 2,800 passwords, and early network pen testing leading to pre-lunch domain admin.
- **Network Scanning**: Kevin reflects on authoring a 40-page Nmap training workbook covering command-line flags, Nmap Scripting Engine plugins, TCP flags (SYN, FIN, RST), and Xmas scans.
- **Hardware & Environment**: References to Fortinet APs, VGA upscalers, HDMI handshake issues with disparate projector models and Mac laptops, and home automation using TP-Link switches and Nest thermostat sensors.

### Takeaways
- Community-driven security conferences rely heavily on dedicated, unpaid volunteers to deliver high-quality, hands-on learning experiences.
- As the cybersecurity field grows and fragments, hands-on mentorship and self-driven learning are critical to preparing the next generation of practitioners without setting them up for failure.

He traces its roots to around 2001, when his work at a state education network exposed public institutions running without basic firewalls. Early on, a commercial SANS training course reshaped his view, and he took those fundamentals back to local audiences. He also describes the conference's storage problem, with years of event gear filling a basement.

On the wider state of security, he argues that firewalls only cover the border, while data loss prevention and many other areas are still neglected. He cites projected ransomware losses above 20 billion dollars and says sysadmins are buried under a steady stream of critical patches and high-severity CVEs. He explains that the organizing committee gathers at a pool after each day of the event, where ideas for future years come from, and that the culture is family friendly with less drinking than some other conferences.

He also shares a physical penetration test that went wrong when a building's security guard confronted his team. They carried authorization paperwork, but the guard would not look at it, and the team left after failing to reach its target and was later tracked down. The main lesson he draws is to carry signed authorization paperwork on every physical test, since it may not calm a nervous guard.

talks.title: 2019 - Keenan Fessler - Evolving Manipulation: Cracking the Combo
talks.teaser: Traces how combination safe locks evolved from simple wheel packs to cam designs, and how each change still leaks clues.
talks.summary:
The talk follows how combination safe locks changed over time, beginning with the basic wheel pack and fence design. In that design a dial spun against the fence reveals gates through feel, so the attacker can note the width of each range and estimate where the gates sit. The speaker points out that some manufacturers' false gates are narrow while the real gate is wider, which changes how the results should be read.

The next stage was the group two design, which added a cam and a nose that stop the fence from riding the wheels. Instead of feeling the fence, the attacker reads the contact points between wheels at set positions, records the left and right values, and graphs them. Spikes and dips in the graph point to a gate, and a high-low test then isolates individual wheels so each number can be confirmed. Group one locks add split cams, spring-loaded parts and plastic wheels, which make the lock harder to feel and much slower to work. Electronic rated locks are touched on briefly.

The talk closes with destructive attacks and the defences against them, such as a spring-loaded lever that drops into place when the back of the lock is blown off. The speaker recommends a book on group two safecracking as a starting point for learners and suggests patent searches and old catalogues for finding details about a particular safe. The main takeaway is that each protection removed one leak but introduced another, and that a lock's rating reflects how long manipulation takes.

talks.title: 2019 - John Pope, James Pope - Hacking Hackers: Sure you can borrow my clicker!
talks.teaser: Demonstrates keystroke injection into wireless Logitech input devices using a cheap radio, and what defenders can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a weakness in wireless presentation clickers, mice and keyboards that use Logitech unifying receivers, which accept injected keystrokes over a 2.4 GHz radio link. The speakers explain how a low-cost USB radio dongle can scan channels, identify devices by their address and send crafted input without any pairing. They describe how the technique surfaced during their own testing, when the captured input turned out to come from their own mouse and keyboard.

The middle of the talk covers demonstrations and related cases. During a Black Hat knock setup, several wireless devices proved vulnerable, and the speakers showed payloads that opened a calculator and ran a PowerShell download. They built an Electron-based tool that runs in the background and can take screenshots, enable the webcam, play sounds and exchange chat messages with the victim through the keyboard. They also reported that Logitech's 2016 fix was incomplete, that a newer patch arrived in 2019, and that some newly shipped devices were still unpatched.

The closing advice is practical. Patch unifying receivers, because the fix is separate from ordinary device driver updates. Use wired input for sensitive presentations, consider a spare laptop for presenting, and look for unexpected wireless receivers on machines in your environment. Treat any unknown input device as untrusted, and test whether your own hardware is affected before assuming it is safe.

talks.title: 2019 - Kyle Feuz - Wireshark: A Beginners Introduction
talks.teaser: Walks through Wireshark basics: baselining traffic, display filters, coloring rules, and spotting an Nmap scan.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a reminder to capture traffic only where you have permission, and it works from existing capture files rather than live capture. Because every network is different, the speaker stresses building a baseline of normal traffic first. What a capture can see depends on the hardware: switches limit what a host sees, so taps or port mirroring may be needed, and wireless capture needs drivers that support promiscuous mode. Statistics such as packets per second and protocol hierarchy give a sense of typical volume.

Profiles keep columns, filters and coloring rules separate, and any packet field can become a column. Display filters narrow the list, but the SSH filter only matches the ports Wireshark decodes as SSH, so SSH on other ports can be missed. Exercises match IP addresses to MAC addresses using ARP replies and identify an SSH server and the UDP protocols in use. Coloring rules are applied top to bottom and only when enabled, highlighting matches while keeping surrounding context.

The final section applies these tools to reconnaissance. ICMP, ARP and reverse DNS lookups each expose different kinds of scanning, and a filter on pointer-type DNS queries reveals an Nmap scan sweeping addresses in sequence. Turning that filter into a red coloring rule makes such activity stand out in baseline traffic. Once a scanning source is found, its IP and MAC addresses can be checked against inventory to decide what to investigate next.

talks.title: 2019 - David Packham
talks.teaser: Shows how DJI drone firmware and settings can be modified to change flight limits and bypass geofencing.
talks.summary:
The talk covers hacking consumer DJI drones, based on the argument that people should be able to change hardware they own. It opens with common questions: whether a drone can be taken over mid-flight, whether Wi-Fi-connected models are exposed, and whether jamming guns can bring one down. An open Wi-Fi access point on a small drone allows easy command injection, while a DJI Spark uses an encrypted link. Jammers mostly trigger return-to-home or landing behaviour.

The speaker then turns to rules and incidents, including the 250-gram weight threshold for lighter drones, no-fly zones, and the April 2019 Gatwick Airport closure, where a couple was arrested and later released. A debug view in DJI's assistant software exposes a parameter list that can be edited to change limits such as height, tilt and no-fly flags. Firmware images can be downloaded, and a tool was shown that loads older signed firmware by forcing the drone into bootloader mode, where loaded modules perform no integrity checks.

The live demo ends with a modified Spark taking off, filming and landing. The main takeaway is that the drone's protection depended on obscurity and signing that could be bypassed, and that changing flight rules raises safety and legal risks for owners.

The talk introduces the statewide information and analysis center in Utah, a fusion center within the state's public safety department. Its cyber role shares threat information with IT staff across state and local government, education, and critical infrastructure, and turns raw indicators of compromise into analysis that decision makers can use. The speaker stresses that information only becomes intelligence once it has been evaluated and placed in context.

The center offers three services: threat notifications drawn from open sources where attackers post stolen accounts or defacement claims, analysis and referrals that move local incidents to state or federal investigators, and federal intelligence products adapted to Utah. One example was a sextortion email campaign, where hundreds of reports were compiled and submitted to the FBI and state investigators. Staff also found three breaches that victims did not know about and notified them, and found hundreds of servers with remote desktop exposed to the internet.

To help organizations build their own threat picture, the speaker pointed to free open sources such as paste sites, defacement mirror archives, and an internet device search service. The talk then listed no-cost federal and partner resources, including a multi-state center with a 24/7 operations center, malware and URL analysis, vulnerability assessments, and incident response, plus InfraGard and sector-specific sharing groups. Cybercrime should be reported to IC3 and the state office, and responders should preserve forensic evidence while fixing a problem.

talks.title: 2019 - Matt Lorimer - What the CTF?
talks.teaser: Explains capture the flag formats and why they help newcomers and professionals, with practical tips for getting started.
talks.summary:
Matt Lorimer argues that capture the flag competitions are worth trying for almost anyone in the field, from people just starting out to experienced staff. He starts by explaining that the term covers many event types: jeopardy-style boards of challenges, attack-and-defense games where teams keep their own services running while taking down opponents, wargames, simulated pentests, and certification exams such as OSEP, which works like a long CTF. He also notes that some conference badges teach real skills, and that companies use CTFs both to build staff capability and to recruit.

He then gives practical advice. Choose a difficulty you can finish, start with beginner-friendly sites such as NeverLand and picoCTF, and use published walkthroughs to learn before writing your own. Find a friend or a team, specialise in an area such as reverse engineering or cryptography, and introduce yourself to people working on the same challenge. He stresses that the learning comes from getting stuck and from going back after the event to understand a solution rather than just collecting points. One example is a team whose contest solution ran too slowly; after the event they optimised it from hours down to minutes. Another is a solver who noticed odd behaviour in a challenge using ffmpeg, which turned out to be a remote code execution bug that was then disclosed responsibly.

He closes by encouraging attendees to give back: write challenges, create walkthroughs, and start local groups or school clubs. He describes a monthly local meetup that draws about 35 people, and argues that sharing knowledge does not reduce anyone's chances in a competition.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation delivered at SaintCON, security engineer and former access control architect Pips (also known as Caden / Kaydan) examines how enterprise Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) access control systems operate, their common architectural weaknesses, and practical exploitation methods. Drawing on professional experience retrofitting and auditing physical security systems, the speaker demonstrates how unencrypted low-frequency card data and sequential issuance patterns expose facilities to badge cloning, proximity skimming, and brute-force attacks, while concluding with defensive measures.

### Key Topics
- **RFID Fundamentals & Form Factors:** RFID functions as short-range, typically powerless one-way communication where an energized reader coil powers a passive card's chip and antenna. Common implementations span low-frequency HID clamshell cards, thin printable badges, medallions, wristbands, zip ties, laundry fabric tags, tracking nails, vehicle tags, and subdermal glass implants.
- **Access Control Data Structure:** Typical low-frequency credentials (e.g., standard HID) transmit minimal plain data to a controller: format length, facility code, and card/serial number. Systems often issue cards sequentially from factory boxes, meaning all authorized cards share a single facility code and adjacent serial IDs.
- **Cloning and Emulation:** Devices such as the Proxmark3 can read existing badges, write credential payloads to blank rewritable cards, or directly emulate valid credentials at a reader without needing physical cards.
- **Brute-Force Exploitation:** Because facility codes remain static across an organization and card numbers increment sequentially, obtaining an inactive or low-privilege credential (or buying a terminated employee's card) allows an attacker to discover the facility code. An automated tool like the Proxmark3 can then cycle through neighboring card numbers until a valid match triggers the physical door latch.

### Technical Details
- **Targeting and Reconnaissance:** In a red teaming scenario, attackers perform open-source intelligence (OSINT) on social media platforms (such as Twitter or Instagram geotag searches for terms like "new badge") to identify badge artwork, layouts, employee names, and security features (e.g., magnetic stripes, holograms). Physical targeting takes place in high-density or close-quarters areas like public transit, elevators, smoking areas, and cafes.
- **Skimming Mechanisms:** Concealed antennas or long-range readers hidden in satchels, messenger bags, or gloves allow attackers to skim badge data unnoticed during casual bumps or close passes.
- **Brute-Force Trade-offs:** While access control controllers typically lack rate-limiting or anti-brute-force controls, brute-forcing at a reader is noisy (audible beeps, mechanical clicking) and can be spotted on centralized monitoring dashboards. Furthermore, an attacker operating blindly may trigger access alarms by guessing the ID of an already badged-in employee (violating passback/stage-badging rules) or an alarmed terminated employee.

### Takeaways
- **Layered Authentication:** Organizations should not rely on simple low-frequency RFID cards as a sole authentication factor. PIN pads, two-factor authentication, physical keys, or guard-assisted verification should supplement electronic access.
- **Operational & Physical Defenses:** Employees should use RFID-blocking sleeves or wallets during non-use hours (as badges are only needed for seconds each day). Organizations should institute strict in-sight badge policies that prohibit wearing credentials off-premises.
- **Visual & Human Verification:** Access control management software should display registered badgeholder photos to front-desk guards upon badging to prevent impersonation, and staff should be trained in friendly verification to question unbadged visitors.

talks.teaser: Explains how security frameworks provide a baseline, and why compliance alone does not make a business secure.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces security frameworks as a way for organizations, including those without a dedicated security team, to set a baseline against attackers ranging from opportunistic individuals to nation-states. The speaker describes a framework as a set of policies and procedures that document a domain such as healthcare data or networking, and sketches a common lifecycle: identify assets, protect them, detect abnormal activity, respond to incidents, and recover.

Before adopting a framework, the speaker recommends listing what the team is responsible for, ranking assets by how critical or sensitive they are, and deciding which risks to accept or fund. Choices should be aligned with business priorities, since leadership supports spending when it sees value, and teams should track where data lives, since regional regulations differ. Planning, reading the full documentation, naming resources, documenting progress and securing executive buy-in are presented as essential. A cautionary story describes a CIS-related configuration tool that locked the speaker out of a machine, illustrating why a framework should be tailored rather than applied blindly.

The closing argument is that compliance is a starting point, not proof of security. Frameworks such as PCI and HIPAA, drawn from the speaker's healthcare and payments background, often make organizations insurable, but they are time-consuming and resource-heavy. The audience should treat them as a foundation to tailor, expect that breaches can happen, and keep improving security as a shared responsibility.

talks.title: 2019 - Karl Sickendick - Reverse Engineering and Code Emulation with Ghidra
talks.teaser: Shows how Ghidra's P-code can be emulated with Python to run a single binary function outside the full program.
talks.summary:
Ghidra, the open-source reverse engineering tool released by the NSA, is introduced first, along with how it works. Its SLEIGH modules lift machine code for many architectures into P-code, an architecture-neutral intermediate language, and the decompiler builds C-like output from that. The speaker covers setup, shared projects that let teams track changes on a Ghidra server, and the basic workflow of importing a binary, running analysis, and enabling P-code in the listing. Comparing x86-64 and ARM64 function prologues shows how P-code makes the exact effect of each instruction easy to read.

Next come ways to improve decompiler output: fixing function signatures and parameter types so changes propagate through the code, and defining custom structures and data types. The talk also covers scripting in Ghidra's built-in Python environment, which runs an older Python 2.7-based runtime, so modern third-party libraries are harder to use. Scripts can query the open program and the current address, and can ask the user for input.

The main demo is P-code emulation, which runs one function without executing the whole program. The target was a function from the NSA's Python Enigma simulator that takes output, key, rotor, plugboard, and input pointers. After the script set up those arguments in memory, the emulation finished in a few minutes and produced the same output as the original binary. The speaker closes by noting limits: system calls are not emulated, and the interface is rough. Emulation fills the gap between static and dynamic analysis when a debugger is impractical, such as for malicious code or hardware without tooling.

talks.title: 2018 - Kyle Feuz - Wireshark: A Beginners Introduction
talks.teaser: Walks through Wireshark basics, from interface and display filters to ARP, IP, TCP and DNS packet analysis.
talks.summary:
This hands-on introductory session teaches attendees how to analyze network traffic in Wireshark using a prepared capture file, rather than capturing live traffic. It opens with a reminder that a capture only shows packets that pass the capture point, so where you sniff matters. The presenter advises against capture filters in most cases, since they can discard evidence you may need later, and recommends learning display filters instead. Profiles are presented as a way to keep interface settings, filters and coloring rules separate for different kinds of analysis.

The middle of the session works through the sample file. Attendees use filters and the protocol hierarchy view to find an SSH server and the UDP protocols in use. The presenter notes that Wireshark only treats traffic as SSH by its port number, so a server on a non-standard port must be added to the protocol preferences. Other sections cover ARP request and reply pairs and how to spot gratuitous ARP, IP fragmentation flags and TTL values, ICMP echo and error messages, DNS query matching, and TCP handshakes, retransmissions and selective acknowledgment. Following TCP streams, exporting HTTP objects and measuring HTTP response times are also demonstrated.

The closing takeaway is practical: keep all traffic in the capture, use display filters and time-delta columns to find slow or unusual exchanges, and watch for Basic authentication and readable cookies in plain HTTP.

talks.title: 2018 - Jeremy Cox - Leverage the Dark Side of your Network
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn unused address space into a darknet that logs scanners and automatically blocks them on a Palo Alto firewall.
talks.summary:
Jeremy Cox, a networking security manager at a school district, explains how to build a darknet: a block of internal addresses with no DNS records, no servers and no legitimate traffic. Because nothing should ever talk to that space, any connection to it is suspicious, and it mainly catches automated scanners such as nmap. He advises sizing the darknet to the available address space, placing it at the start or end of the range so sequential scans hit it early, and routing it through the firewall.

The middle of the talk covers the Palo Alto configuration. A darknet zone is tied to an interface and virtual router, and a deny policy sends matching traffic to a syslog-ng server on a Linux host using a custom log format. On the server, a filter writes firewall logs to their own file, which is rotated daily and kept for 14 days. A PHP script served by Apache extracts the unique scanning addresses for each day and exposes them as an external dynamic list. The firewall pulls the current list every five minutes, and the speaker blocks listed addresses for three days. A second log profile records what gets blocked, and a rule denies traffic from the lists.

The talk closes with cautions. Dynamic block lists can catch legitimate users, so exceptions and close monitoring are needed, and spoofed source addresses are a risk. Panorama can push the lists to many firewalls at once. Practitioners should keep the darknet space genuinely clean and watch what their lists pull in.

talks.title: 2018 - Samuel Kimmons - Following the Bread Crumbs... How an Investigation Should Change O2
talks.teaser: Walks through decoding layered base64 and hex obfuscation in a packet capture to reveal a hidden malicious redirect.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an analyst who followed a standard checklist on an alert drawn from a packet capture and found nothing obviously malicious. The speaker argues that rigid, checkbox-style procedures leave analysts unable to examine individual data points, and that real intrusions rarely announce themselves.

The speaker then reruns the same capture with a looser approach. A blob of data turns out to be base64 encoded, and it decodes to JavaScript whose variables are hex encoded. Decoding those reveals a link to an executable on a malicious domain and a redirect to another site. Tools such as CyberChef are demonstrated, and the speaker notes that built-in decoding in security devices may not go deep enough. Other examples cover benign techniques turned against defenders, including DNS queries carrying encoded command-and-control data and text records used to smuggle script that runs in a browser. Heavy alert volumes make it hard for tier-one analysts to reverse layered obfuscation.

The recommended method treats each data point as a stepping off point that raises questions, with the answers feeding back into the investigation. The speaker ties this back to his own early career, when a similar alert turned out to be cryptojacking malware hosted on a baking recipe site. The takeaway is to adapt the methodology to the evidence rather than follow fixed steps, and not to assume tooling will catch everything.

talks.title: 2018 - Chris Mather
talks.teaser: Explains how quantum computers threaten today's public-key encryption, and surveys quantum key exchange and post-quantum defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the fear that quantum computers will break the encryption protecting today's networks. The speaker gives a non-technical primer on quantum mechanics, covering electrons and photons, superposition, spin and entanglement, and explains how these properties relate to qubits. Quantum supremacy, the point where such machines outpace classical ones, is estimated at 60 to 100 qubits.

The attack side covers data collected today and held until capable hardware exists. Citing a 2016 NIST report and a 2015 NSA recommendation, the speaker notes that RSA, elliptic curve and DSA are exposed, while AES and hashing resist better with larger keys. Hardware progress includes a 72-qubit Google system, a 50-qubit IBM machine and D-Wave's 2048-qubit annealer. The defensive side covers lattice-based and hash-based algorithms plus photon key exchange, where interception disturbs the key. Long distances need relays or satellites, as in a Chinese experiment.

The talk ends with hands-on resources, including Microsoft's Q# language, IBM's cloud quantum service and an open-source board game. The main takeaway is to strengthen encryption now and plan a move to post-quantum algorithms before the hardware arrives.

talks.title: 2018 - Andrew Brandt - Hey, You Got Your SQL In My Honeypot!
talks.teaser: Traces a persistent attack on a fake SQL Server honeypot, from its 122 setup steps to the crypto miners it delivered.
talks.summary:
Andrew Brandt runs a malware research lab from home and places a honeypot on his DMZ to gather threat intelligence. The honeypot imitates a Microsoft SQL Server, and the talk follows one attack that kept arriving over the TDS protocol on port 1433. About 77% of that port's traffic came from China a year earlier, and nearly 85% over a later two-month window.

Each attack ran in a single TCP session, usually under about 3.5 minutes and fewer than 500 packets. The attacker logged in as an administrator, replaced built-in stored procedures, and used them to edit registry keys, strip Image File Execution Options and Group Policy restrictions, and set SQL Server Agent to start automatically. Hex-encoded blobs were written out as executables, security product process names were killed, account passwords were changed and locked, and traces were deleted. Brandt counted about 122 steps, many of them repeated several ways.

The final payloads were Windows crypto miners. Some antivirus engines labelled them Mirai, which Brandt considered likely imprecise, since the command-and-control domains had been used by Mirai operators. Pivoting through a relationship-mapping tool and a new GitHub project called Danger Zone, he linked domains, IP addresses and samples, and one sample fetched its instructions from a blog on a large Chinese web platform. He closed by urging admins to disable remote desktop and patch, and noted that long-running miners can overheat and damage hardware.

talks.title: 2018 - Inside the Defcon 26 Mad Max Valhalla Self Driving Car Challenge
talks.teaser: Walks through the Car Hacking Village's Mad Max CAN bus challenge and building self-driving RC cars with the Donkey Car project.
talks.summary:
David Owens recaps the Mad Max challenge run by the Car Hacking Village at DEF CON 26 and the Donkey Car project behind its self-driving race. The contest had two parts. In the Robo Car challenge, players intercepted CAN bus traffic from a remote-accessible RC car, separated the messages by function, replayed them, and then used those commands to drive a course and hold a parking spot for a minute. The head-to-head Donkey Car race reduced points for hitting cones or walls or needing pilot help.

The second half covers Donkey Cars, an open community project that began in the San Francisco Bay Area and runs a Python driving loop with drive, train and autopilot modes. Owens defines AI, machine learning, neural networks, overfitting and data cleaning for newcomers. He outlines the workflow: calibrate steering and throttle in a config file, record roughly 10,000 to 30,000 camera images paired with throttle and steering values, remove bad data, train a model (about an hour for 30,000 images on his laptop), then run it on the car. For races, he prefers a constant throttle over full autopilot, since autopilot can learn to outpace the driver.

He closes with a simulator option for people without hardware, community Slack channels, and setup documentation for Mac, Linux and Windows. The practical lessons are that clean data matters more than sheer volume, and that batteries fade after about 15 minutes of full driving.

talks.title: 2018 - James Pope
talks.teaser: Walks through an attacker's view of phishing, leaked passwords and domain escalation, with defensive steps to reduce each risk.
talks.summary:
This Security 101 session asks attendees to adopt an attacker's mindset. The speaker recounts how, as a child, he got around locked-down school computers by taking hardware apart and booting alternative software, which taught him to look past what a system was meant to allow. He then mocks a how-to article that promised to make someone a hacker in five steps, and a viral list of supposed hacker traits, arguing that the real skill is seeing a situation differently.

Moving to his consulting work, he says phishing is the most common way in. He describes fake login portals and a fake website-voting lure that collected credentials, including from administrators, and notes that payload delivery is often blocked by controls. He explains how breached password dumps still reveal reused credentials, how internet search engines expose services such as remote desktop, and how a single compromised machine can lead to a domain when a privileged user is logged in there. Macro-enabled Word documents, unpatched SMB, and ransomware and cryptocurrency-era attacks round out the examples.

For defenders, his takeaways are to verify unexpected requests through a known channel, block macros by policy, use long passphrases checked against breach lists, enable multi-factor authentication, and remove local admin rights. He also recommends limiting user access, keeping tested backups, patching promptly, and publishing SPF and DKIM records. Layered controls and security awareness training help contain a single compromise.

talks.title: 2018 - Josh Galvez
talks.teaser: Explains how the Hackers Challenge puzzle board scores and plays, then solves a simple Caesar cipher as an example.
talks.summary:
This beginner orientation to the Hackers Challenge puzzle board at SAINTCON is aimed at attendees new to capture-the-flag style puzzles. The speaker first explains the mechanics: players register on the game site with the email address from their conference registration, which also drives scoring. Each puzzle opens at 10,000 points and drops as others solve it, so one puzzle fell to 5,000 and then 3,333 points as more players finished. Flags usually appear as a text string at the end of a solved puzzle, and wrong guesses carry no penalty.

The middle section covers tools and approach. Most needed utilities already live on a laptop or in a Linux distribution such as Kali, plus basic shell utilities for handling data. Recognizing formats matters most: a string ending in equals signs suggests base64, fixed-length strings suggest hashes, and file headers or trailing data can reveal hidden archives or audio. The speaker recommends following security news, searching unfamiliar terms, reading archived walkthroughs from earlier contests, and asking other players how they approached a puzzle rather than for the answer.

To demonstrate, the speaker works through a 100-level classic crypto puzzle whose description mentions a Roman emperor's cipher. Searching leads to the Caesar cipher, and a rotation solver on a cipher toolkit site exposes readable text at one shift, revealing the answer. The closing advice is to avoid overthinking easy puzzles, troubleshoot step by step as with a broken network, and use the hands-on hacker labs environment for practice attacking Windows and Linux machines.

talks.title: 2018 - Colin Jackson
talks.teaser: A beginner class covers pin-tumbler mechanics, tension, binding, and picks, then sends attendees to lockpick village practice.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames lock picking as an accessible entry point into security and a practical skill for physical penetration work, where weak hardware can undo expensive network controls. He contrasts this classroom-style overview with hands-on coaching at the conference lockpick village and points newcomers to TOOOL materials for clearer visuals.

The core lesson walks through pin-tumbler anatomy—key pins, driver pins, and the shear line—and how picking recreates key alignment without a key. Binding and light tension receive the most emphasis, along with pitfalls such as overlifting. Single-pin picking, raking, and half-diamond techniques are explained, plus how to estimate pin count and place tension at the bottom of the keyway for feedback and reach.

Ethics come first: do not pick locks you do not own or still depend on; practice on spare locks instead. The talk closes with village practice ladders, upcoming escape-room and head-to-head contests, starter kit suggestions, reading lists, and examples of nastier high-security locks worth studying later.

### Overview
In this talk, Erich Ficker outlines a practical blueprint for launching and advancing a career in penetration testing and information security. Drawing on personal experiences and industry realities, he discusses essential baseline technical knowledge, self-guided lab practices, certifications, and the realities of interviewing and career navigation across different organizational environments.

### Key Topics
- **Foundational IT and Networking Skills**: A solid background in IT infrastructure—such as understanding web servers, database communications, DMZs, and networking fundamentals—is essential. Security professionals should know basic IT well enough to step into an IT role temporarily if needed.
- **Essential Tools and Scripting**: Practical mastery of everyday tools including Nmap, Burp Suite, Nessus, Netcat, and SQLMap, alongside practical scripting languages like Python or Ruby to automate tasks or parse target lists.
- **Hands-on Labs and Exploit Analysis**: Setting up virtual machines to experiment with newly announced vulnerabilities, researching public proofs of concept from repositories like Exploit Database, and understanding why specific exploits work (e.g., MS17-010 / SMBv1 or MS08-067).
- **Certifications and Industry Best Practices**: Using entry certs such as Security+ or networking certifications to bridge background gaps, and familiarizing oneself with standard compliance and best-practice frameworks such as ISO 27001 and PCI.
- **Navigating the Job Market and Career Growth**: Handling interviews to build resilience, delivering value in an initial analyst role, and understanding the trade-offs between smaller companies and large organizations (such as the Big Four).

### Technical Details
- **Reconnaissance and Scanning**: Heavy emphasis on Nmap for targeted scanning using command-line switches and Lua-based Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE) scripts rather than relying solely on Zenmap or heavy vulnerability scanners.
- **Application and Vulnerability Testing**: Burp Suite is highlighted as the premier application security testing tool, with the free tier covering the majority of necessary manual testing capabilities. Vulnerability scanning tools like Nessus provide complementary assessment capability.
- **Exploitation Concepts**: Hands-on dissection of proof-of-concept exploits to adjust parameters like IP addresses and understand vulnerabilities such as SMBv1 issues (MS17-010) or remote code execution flaws (MS08-067 via Metasploit).

### Takeaways
Early in a cybersecurity career, dedicating significant personal time to hands-on experimentation, home labs, and reading threat intelligence blogs or disclosures accelerates progression out of entry-level analyst roles. Professionals should focus on solving problems for their teams, cross-training across disciplines (such as physical penetration testing or lock picking), maintaining professional humility, and remaining willing to change employers if opportunities for growth and upward mobility become stagnant.

talks.teaser: Walks through common PCI compliance myths and gray areas that assessors see in real organizations.
talks.summary:
Jonathan Smith, a PCI assessor with a consulting firm, presents a set of common myths and gray areas he sees while assessing organizations for PCI compliance. He stresses that assessors and companies are on the same side, aiming to protect the payment ecosystem. Early topics cover configuration drift, which centralized management tools can counter, and VoIP systems, which fall in scope whenever cardholder data is taken over phone calls.

The middle covers logging and access control for custom applications and patching of third-party products such as Java and Adobe Reader, which often fall outside Windows update tooling. Change management applies to all changes, not only code. Service providers, including MPLS carriers, need clear responsibility matrices and attestations of compliance. Business teams should help map where cardholder data flows, since staff may take card numbers over email. Shared administrative accounts clash with individual accountability, so a designated emergency account holder can reset the shared password under personal credentials. Multi-factor authentication must apply at each administrative layer.

The closing section addresses scan timing, with no more than 90 days between quarterly scans, and notes that organizations define what counts as a significant change. Vulnerability scanner output needs human review for false positives and under-rated findings. Sampling can validate compliance but cannot be used to apply requirements across a population. The key takeaway is that PCI is an everyday discipline rather than an annual report, and that an assessor cannot make an organization compliant on its own.

The talk opens with a few light stories before turning to amygdala hijacking, the idea that the fast emotional part of the brain can react before the slower rational part catches up. The speaker explains that the amygdala tends to win this race, which can push people into poor decisions during social engineering attempts. A simple model of three brain parts, the neocortex, the limbic system and the primal brain, frames the risk.

The strategies include recognizing feelings, talking them through with someone trusted, reviewing past reactions to spot patterns and triggers, journaling, setting specific goals with an accountability partner, practicing everyday emotional situations and watching for traps. Threat modeling is presented as identifying risks and planning around them, such as taking a different road to avoid a slow street. Stories illustrate these points: a stranger in a home improvement store accusing the speaker of a shooting, a mystery noise at home that turned out to be a battery-powered air freshener, and a long repair of a wireless device under deadline pressure in a parking lot.

The talk closes with a volunteer on stage asked to describe a recent emotional reaction, showing how being watched raises the stakes. The main takeaway is that managing these responses takes repeated practice rather than a single fix, and that everyday situations are a good place to build control. The question period also covered experiments with pushpins and signs.

talks.title: Chris Larsen (2017) - Phishing Trends are Changing: From Personal to Organizational
talks.teaser: Shows how reusable phishing kits harvest email credentials, shifting attacks from brand logins toward organizational data.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how phishing has moved from mass-market lures toward attacks that harvest email logins. The speaker separates generic phishing, spearphishing and mass malicious spam, and notes that many reports labeled as phishing are really plain spam. Phishing kits, packaged as zip files with server-side code, can reportedly be bought for about ten bucks and need only an email address changed before being hosted on compromised servers or cheap hosts.

To study the kits, the research team used a screenshot-matching project called DolphinView alongside a content-based matcher. Examples included a Google Docs lure and a kit with a legal-documents folder that showed a protected PDF and asked the victim for their email provider and password, even though the lure mimicked Adobe. Many kits copied pages that were years out of date, yet still collected credentials. Across the samples, PayPal ranked first, followed by Google Docs, Dropbox and several banks, with DocuSign appearing unexpectedly high. DolphinView data for one month showed most phishing traffic aimed at email or cloud logins rather than classic financial sites.

The talk then connected this to shadow data, the enterprise information stored in unsanctioned cloud services. Survey respondents estimated 40 to 50 cloud apps in use, while traffic logs for the average enterprise showed 928 in late 2016. This links personal email credentials to organizational exposure, since company data is spread across outside services. The talk was set to close by combining both parts and offering recommendations.

talks.title: Michael Fowkes (2017) - In Our world, Data is the Silver Bullet
talks.teaser: Shows how passive web crawling and public datasets map sprawling cloud and SaaS footprints for continuous, scalable security assessments.
talks.summary:
Enterprises no longer keep assets in a single data center: hosting spreads across cloud providers, SaaS vendors, and countries, which makes classic scoped pen tests and slow questionnaire cycles hard to scale and weak on assurance. The speaker frames traditional manage-protect-detect-respond matrices against devices, applications, networks, data, and users, then contrasts cheap documentation reviews with costly on-site work, arguing for approaches that raise confidence without matching full enterprise assessment prices.

The core method treats a single website visit as a rich data source. HTTP responses, headers, JavaScript libraries, DNS, MX records, TLS settings, and WHOIS and geo lookups chain into discovery of additional hosts, hosting providers, and countries—with no port scanning or exploitation. Two Fortune 100 examples start from one hostname and company name only: one data-processing firm yields hundreds of internet-facing servers, many providers, and measurable gaps such as end-of-life software, certificate problems, weak SSL, and missing email authentication; an insurer shows similar scale and misconfiguration rates, giving objective evidence against polished policy answers.

The closing message is that footprinting must include IaaS, SaaS, outsourced IT, and third- and fourth-party links, mining crawl logs with public threat and registration data and analytics for permissionless, continuous visibility. Practitioners should extend assessment scope to every place data actually lives, not only the owned data center.

talks.title: Jon Jarvis (2017) - The Surveillance Capitalism will continue, until Morale Improves
talks.teaser: Surveys how companies and governments collect personal data via faces, location, devices and browsers, plus ways to resist.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from surveillance capitalism, a term coined in 2015 by a Harvard Business School professor for collecting behavioural data to predict and shape what people do for revenue. The speaker argues this differs from older surveillance in its scale, its motive (selling to people rather than investigating crime) and its methods, since ordinary connected devices now gather data constantly. Privacy is framed as control over what you share, with whom, and whether you can withdraw consent, rather than as hiding wrongdoing.

The middle section works through collection methods with a specific case for each. Facial recognition was shown matching a comic character despite a disguise, scanning faces at a casino to find self-excluded gamblers, and gating entry to a gas station and a jewelry store. Geofencing was used to serve advertising to phones inside an abortion clinic and to flag city regulators who entered government offices while calling an Uber car. Other examples covered browser canvas fingerprinting, cross-device tracking, ultrasonic beacons, in-store Wi-Fi tracking, and a data broker that sold lists of people identified as Muslim.

The closing part looks at defences and trade-offs. Suggested steps include restricting app permissions, blocking ads and trackers, turning off location, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and paying with cash where possible. The speaker says most of these are only partial stopgaps, and urges anyone building data systems to collect less and design privacy in from the start. Surveillance footage that helped identify a suspect in a library assault was presented as the case where wider monitoring seems justified.
